ATHANASIUS KIRCHER.
OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS.

[Large decorative initial Q containing a figure] ALMOST four
lustra have now passed,
Most Serene King, in which
course of time, under
the most fortunate [auspices] of glorious me-
mory of FERDINAND III,
Caesar, Your Best and Greatest father,
in the literary arena for my
* 2 in-

--- Page 4 ---
I strive according to my modest talent; in which endeavors the Most Wise Emperor [Ferdinand III] shone forth with an example so rare among Princes, both in the studies of other good arts and especially in promoting the publication of my works, so that what Plutarch relates long ago concerning Alexander and Aristotle (whether the fruitfulness of Aristotle's genius in conceiving so many offspring of wisdom, or the industry of Alexander acting as midwife in bringing them to light, contributed greater benefit to the Literary World, it was doubted) – that very thing I would dare to affirm with much better right concerning the incredible zeal and solicitude of the August Emperor FERDINAND III in promoting letters. The Most Wise Prince had heard that I possessed some works of more profound learning, perhaps not unworthy of the public good, destined for the press; yet, what prevented them from seeing the desired light was both the lack of necessary expenses for publication, and the author being deprived of all auxiliary help

--- Page 5 ---
...and that the lack of a protector was the cause. Wherefore, lest the efforts of genius conceived with so much labor, and the store of literary merchandise acquired with so many toils, should go to ruin, he, with that clemency inherent in his Imperial mind, soon deigned to extend his generous right hand of benevolence to his client, and both by letters packed with weighty arguments, and by the provision of an annual subsidy, and other more-than-royal aids, he not only incited the one languishing for the efforts of the enterprise he had undertaken with the immense stimuli of such favor, but also completely raised up the one wavering under the excessive burden of cares; and lest he omit anything of those things which seemed likely to be advantageous to my undertaking, he also, by benevolent communication, supplied some treasures of more recondite knowledge, drawn from the fertile storehouse of his own genius, partly for the adornment of my works, and partly for the increase of more curious learning. So that therefore, even by this very thing, by a rare example of Imperial beneficence, I learned,

--- Page 6 ---
...rim, nothing lies hidden in the inner sanctuaries of the disciplines so difficult, perplexing, impenetrable, and finally, in everyone's opinion, impossible (ἀδύνατον), but that a Prince, conspicuous for the praise of munificence and benevolence, can extort it, even by a mere nod, from those whose spirit, as if by a certain weight, is driven to perform great and arduous tasks in literary pursuits.

I now turn to You, O King, Great Son of a Great Parent, and glorious offspring of an August House. For since the world acknowledges that the manifestations of paternal virtues—by which your pious and wise Parent drew the entire world into admiration—have flowed into you in a most abundant propagation, as if by a certain hereditary right; and since it wonders at a certain immense vigor of spirit, divinely bestowed upon You in Your Royal person, most opportune both for cultivating the study of Wisdom and for pursuing its cultivators with every favor. Among others, I too, the least, approach Your Sa-

--- Page 7 ---
I take refuge at Your Majesty's sacred altars, relying on this hope and the confidence of a sincere spirit, that whatever fruit the Republic of Letters may expect in the future from my humble person, all of it, just as it was begun and conceived under the fortunate patronage of Your Most Wise Parent, so also may it be brought to completion by Your Majesty's benevolent influence and generous support, even with the added interest of my studies. He, while among the living, had especially encouraged that immense work, which is entitled 'The Subterranean World,' inasmuch as it is admirable for the most hidden effects of nature, if it is completed as it deserves. Nevertheless, since that work, hindered by various misfortunes over time, could not be completed in every respect, I have decided in advance to dedicate this present small work, as a kind of pledge for the future work, to the immortal splendor of Your Name. But if you look upon it with the benevolent eyes of Your Clemency, truly, I, by this new act of kindness, will be encouraged to undertake greater things...

--- Page 8 ---
...to undertake greater things, and grant that, as if spurred by some goad, I may rise up, and as he says, *“I shall strike the stars with my lofty head.”* And certainly it is fitting that you should have it instilled and persuaded in your Great Mind, that nothing can be more effective for perpetuating the immortality of the name of Princes and Kings than to have zealously favored wise men (whose multitude is the health of the world). And that this may happen, I pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that He may adorn your Royal breast with excellent laws, and fill it with works worthy of praise and abundant wisdom, and protect it when filled; that in great matters the power of the Most High may guide, assist, and defend you, and accumulate upon you every fullness of royal happiness. Farewell, Great King; may you long and greatly endure, for yourself, the Church, and God.
At Rome, 1st November 1657.

# PREFACE
# TO THE READER.
# PART ONE
### On the Scope of the Ecstatic Journey Undertaken.

[Decorative Initial I]HE ecstatic journey,
kind Reader, which into
the celestial Worlds of a higher Nature,
under the faithful direction and
auspices of Cosmiel, I had
long since undertaken, soon
made public, as I learned it was received with
greater approval by learned men than I had expected,
so it added no small stimuli and spurs to me for another
expedition of a new and unheard-of journey. But what
journey will you say? Do you wish to know, Reader? I will explain
it to you in a few words: I undertake a journey, undoubtedly far
☩ ☩ more sublime

--- Page 10 ---
...doubtless far more sublime, to be traversed with a smaller chariot than that in which they say Proserpina was once snatched by Pluto, into the hitherto unknown realms of the subterranean world, into the innermost recesses of the Geocosmic Monarchy; a truly daring, unprecedented, and a deed perhaps to be feared even by the heart of Alcides. Therefore, should I dare to undertake a journey that no mortal to this day has—I will not say attempted and trodden with footsteps—but not even penetrated by the imagination of the human mind? I dare it, I dare, I say, to undertake it, not so much undertaken by my own will, as extorted by the armed entreaty of illustrious men; and although I well know that this undertaking proposed by me can seem, in the hearts of those who, devoid of practical experience and knowledge of things, are accustomed to weigh matters only according to their outermost surface, as it is usually said, more similar to some Utopia than to a true narration of a journey, nevertheless I am not deterred by anything; indeed, among the followers of true philosophy, who...

--- Page 11 ---
...nevertheless I am not deterred; indeed, among the followers of true philosophy, what they might desire.
Therefore, let us prepare our-
selves for the Rhombus. Just as some philosophers, deceived by a
false persuasion, believe that the mass of the earthly globe was
formed and compacted by God the Earth-creator from the mud of the earth, as if
by chance rather than by a definite plan and a fortuitous heap of mud; than
they think it was, so too they stubbornly persuade themselves that it exists,
devoid of all internal arrangement of chambers, all distribution of nature's
hidden recesses, and all aqueduct
conduits, condensed solely by a filling of slime, mud, and sedi-
ment, no differently than a cheese curd,
truly consolidated as a kind of useless weight of the earth.
Indeed, an opinion so much more unworthy of natural philosophers, as
the dogma they profess is more futile and more ridi-
culous. I know that during the course of this enlight-
ened century, there have been men illustrious in the cultivation of geographical study,
who have diligently toiled to explain the external face of the Geocosm
with truly excellent effort, and no less
praise and immortality of name; yet no one has been found
who has, I will not say, penetrated, but not even reached with the mind, the internal
structure of the earth and the hidden mysteries of underlying
nature. Since, therefore, it has been so prepared for me by nature,
that no one so much in the nature of things is ab-
[ornament: two crosses] 2 di-

--- Page 12 ---
...ditus and obscure an effect shines forth without my burning with the de-
sire of knowing and penetrating its causes, and whose hidden rational
principles, if I do not fully attain by tireless mental
scrutiny, at least I shall place praise in the commendable effort
of the attempt itself. Hence it arose that I turned my mind's
eyes especially to the structure of the subterranean World, hitherto
neglected either because of nature's inaccessible hiding places,
and ignored because of the insuperable difficulties in penetrating
it. Indeed, I thought it impossible but that just as God
and nature do nothing in vain, so the supreme
Wisdom of the World-Architect, in elaborating it with wonderful art,
and in rightly arranging it according to an architectural rule,
and in distributing it into innumerable receptacles of elements
for the necessary uses of all nature, exercised a certain ineffable
industry. For which reason, stimulated by the usual ardor
of my working intellect, I left no stone unturned, so that,
as far as possible, I might penetrate somewhat into the
so hidden constitution of things lying hidden in the Subterranean World.
By no means did I neglect those otherwise opportune
and weighty, and lucid things which seemed to contribute to conceiving
the interior state of the earth, and which from various Wri-
ters

--- Page 13 ---
...from various writers' records I had gathered, but I would not have been content with mere indications, unless I too should elaborate upon the 'Sparta' of hidden truth, established by the investigation of my own experience and [handwritten: autopsy]. Therefore, whatever rare, unusual, and paradoxical things I encountered in the records of geographical accounts, which concerned the constitution of both the entire globe and particular regions, I extracted and noted down with the greatest diligence. The wonderful natural phenomena discovered during oceanic expeditions, in the finding of new regions and unknown seas, I collected and weighed with equal care. I wondered at the manifold movements of the Ocean, and also the regular reciprocations of its ebb and flow. I was astonished by the unstable alternation of currents in whirlpools and Euripi; I was terrified by the inexplicable depth of abysses in several places; I stood astonished at the hidden insinuation of the Ocean into the innermost bowels of mountains and subterranean parts, at the absorption of many rivers in one place, and their regurgitation in another far distant region; and likewise at the connection of lakes with subterranean mountain reservoirs, as well as of the entire Ocean with other seas, lakes, rivers, streams, and springs.

--- Page 14 ---
...springs, I first suspected that some unknown secret dealings were being carried out. Nor did I stop there; I investigated the innermost recesses of metallic mines, in order to explore the incredible industry of nature in its dealings. And lest I seem to have omitted anything, I ascended Etna, explored Stromboli, and also Vesuvius, into which I was admitted some distance, and measured with exact care the craters of each, and the hidden workings of the caves, both to observe more closely the inaccessible origin of seething nature, and to deduce from them conclusions appropriate to my purpose, which I investigated with the impulse of an ardent spirit, yet not without the greatest danger to my life. Indeed, all these having been exactly surveyed, it can scarcely be said how great an admiration for the wonders of the things observed seized my mind. And how ardent a desire to inquire into the causes followed that admiration! Hence, while I more exactly compare individual things with individual things, having reduced them to the crucible of the combinatorial art, I discovered that the inner structure of the Geocosm, or terrestrial globe, is certainly much different, and has a constitution entirely different from the common conception of men; inasmuch as in its skillful arrangement, eternal wisdom did not mi-

--- Page 15 ---
...in the skillful adornment of which eternal wisdom did not labor with less industry than in the construction of the human body, distinguished by so many workshops of vital members, equipped with so many ducts of veins, nerves, and fibers, and pierced by so many blind siphons of passages. So that, therefore, that work, long since promised to the Republic of Letters, which is entitled *Mundus Subterraneus* (Subterranean World) – for which I now toil with the elaboration of many years, and for the sake of investigating which I have undergone so many dangers of labors and perils in exploring the workshops of Subterranean Nature (and of which this present treatise serves merely as a Prodromus) – cannot triumph under a more suitable title. Since whatever is seen diffused with a certain infinite variety of things in the entire machine of the World, that appears contracted, as it were, into a kind of epitome in the Geocosm.

You have, therefore, Reader, my intention in producing this Prodromus of the Subterranean World. In it, if you do not find yourself everywhere satisfied, I would wish you to ascribe that not so much to me, as to the Prodromus, which is hastening towards the most abundant subject matter of the future work. Indeed, in that [future work], whatever here was either omitted due to brevity of time, or hindered by difficulty, or by variety or multitude con-

--- Page 16 ---
...confused, arranged in order, freed from the encountered rocks of difficulties, and also heaped up and adorned with a manifold apparatus of experiments and authorities, as if in a certain treasury of all nature, I am confident you will find it with significant interest. Furthermore, just as in the Celestial Journey, I used the guidance of the simulated Cosmiel for exploring the inaccessible secrets of Superior nature, so also in this Journey of the Subterranean World, I decided to proceed by a method entirely parallel to the former, so that therefore you are not moved by raptures, ecstasies, familiarity with Genii, and similar dictates of speech from men agitated by God. For the Reader should persuade himself that I have used these [things] for no other purpose than both to season the reading with various intellectual diversions, and to explain the individual works of nature more easily and clearly, through questions and answers made back and forth, under these allegorical coverings of things and words.

And so I would wish him to consider this whole commentary nothing other than a certain profound agitation of the mind, diffused into the more recondite repositories of nature, which, as they are hidden and most remote from the comprehension of human intellect, so with a great fervor of mind, and
                                                                  anxious

--- Page 17 ---
anxious with a certain solicitude of a fervent intellect,
that they need to be penetrated, only he can be ignorant of this,
who has never attempted the labyrinths of this kind of philosophy.
Finally, because in exploring all these things, the sole aim of Divine glory
ought to have been set before me, namely that all things
might be led back to that place whence, as from the origin of all good
things, they flowed forth, lest the labor undertaken by
us in this discussion should be unfruitful for the pious
Reader, it seemed good to always insert something
for the nourishment of the soul into our reasonings, in the manner of the
Ascetics, and to construct a certain Mystical ladder,
by which a pious mind might be able to ascend,
through the visible things that have been made, to obtain the abundance
of invisible, never-perishing goods, so that while
it rises from virtue to virtue through the contemplation of things
created by Eternal Wisdom for the sole use of man,
it may finally reach the summit of all happiness, which is the God of
Gods in Sion, who therefore is always praised,
blessed beyond measure, always loved with the affection of all
possible creatures, for everlasting eternities.

PART TWO.

On the Cause and Order of this Little Work.

[Large decorative initial N] EST the reader, deceived by the novelty of an exotic title in the inscription of this little work, should immediately hesitate, doubtful and perplexed, at first glance; in this place, with the sincerity that is fitting, and also with the brevity of words that I can manage, I will opportunely explain the reason for my undertaking.

Therefore, since for a long time now I have been urged by renowned men, through continuous requests in letters, for the publication of a work long since promised (which is entitled *Mundus Subterraneus*); but the aforementioned work, as it is very full with a variety and abundance of hitherto unexplored arguments, so it also requires more leisure and a greater abundance of time than one might believe for so many hidden causes of things, for

--- Page 19 ---
...so many miracles of Nature, which had to be explored not without great daring of spirit, not without innumerable attempts of previous experiments, seemed to demand as extremely necessary [this leisure and time]; hence it happened that the work, now as if established at its peak, both on account of the cruel tyranny of the pestilential plague, which was dominating Italy with a great slaughter of mortals, and other calamities of these warlike times, and also on account of the lamentable death of Ferdinand III, Emperor, a truly most munificent patron, always encountered new and new delays; to which, with the addition of a necessary lack of support, it was not only greatly delayed, but, as if stunned and stupefied by an unlucky throw of the dice, it had to be suspended for some time, until the hope of a better fate should shine upon it. Nevertheless, lest that work, enveloped in the common whirlwind of evils, might seem to be extinguished and buried together, and lest the ardent desires of those awaiting it should fade with a longer delay; this present small work, in which the series of matters to be treated in the preparation of the Great Work would be presented only in general, either for exploring the judgments of more skilled men concerning the plan of my undertaking, or for acquiring some opportune support for the said Work,
[† † †] 2 con-

--- Page 20 ---
...prepare [it]. But what kind of support, you will say? In a few words, I reveal to you the sum of my wishes. Led and taught by long experience, I have come to know that certain wonderful effects, by which the nature of things plays in the world, are so diffused through all climates of the world that scarcely any territory is so small as not to exhibit some exotic and utterly unusual spectacle of playful nature, the core of which hidden reasons, just as it resides in the innermost recess of things, so also it is finally attained only by a long and profound scrutiny of the Mind, through the various laws of combinatorial rule; concerning which, having been made more certain by various sources, since I had rightly recognized that such a mass of things is not the work of one man without the contribution of others who might supply me with the necessary provisions: for this reason, I decided that a literary exchange should be established with Physicians, Chemists, and other Masters of more recondite philosophy; so that what (information) from them concerning the nature of certain particular places, and the native constitution of terrestrial parts, and of other prodigious effects, which (are found) in the exotic qualities of springs and hot baths, in the hidden properties of the winds peculiar to each place, in minerals...

--- Page 21 ---
...and also in metallic bodies, as well as in various saps, oils, and other liquids which certain soils exude, and finally in animals and plants, where the Economy of nature manifests itself, I might gather for myself a huge quantity of the aforementioned things, both to establish the arguments proposed in my great work on a more solid foundation, and for the splendor of the work.
For this being accomplished, I hoped that nature, which has its very rich workshops established in the hidden recesses of the Subterranean World, and in them, with perpetual motion, works intent on the generation of things, might be explained in an easier way, and the causes of unusual effects, which so greatly vex the minds of physicists, might finally be revealed to the great benefit of the Republic of Letters. Here you have the reason for my plan, described in a few words, considering such a great mass of things.
      As for the order of this present Work, I will likewise explain it briefly. The small work, as you see, is divided into three Dialogues; the first of which, with the interlocutors Hydriele and Theodidactus, treats of Water as the universal principle of things, and its necessity and utility in the nature of things; which, as I had long ago composed it by Caesar's command, so indeed, opportunely, it serves as a kind of vestibule

--- Page 22 ---
...which, as I had long ago composed it by Caesar's command, so indeed opportunely I made it a sort of vestibule for the two following Dialogues, and I judged that a certain chief thing should be placed before them; so that what this predecessor touches upon only under a certain universal reasoning, the following ones, with Interlocutors Cosmiel and Theodidact, might explain by the investigation of proximate causes.

And these are the matters concerning which we thought you, dear Reader, should first be advised. Furthermore, if you find anything in this treatise worthy of praise, attribute it to God, to whom alone I live and serve; if anything is faulty and deficient, I would wish you to attribute it to me, as one subject to the human condition; finally, if anything better occurs to you, which could be useful to my work, I earnestly beg you to impart it to me sincerely and candidly, laying aside all perversity of affection; and I, to whom nothing is more important than to be taught by everyone, solemnly promise that I will not be unmindful of the favor rendered, and will duly commend your name.

Farewell and favor my undertakings.

IOAN-

# DIALOGUE I.
## Concerning the Element of Water, & the Universal Principle of Things.
### *With Hydriel and Theodidact as Interlocutors.*

# CHAPTER I.
### *Concerning the Necessity and Utility of the Watery Element in the Nature of Things.*

[A decorative horizontal divider consisting of five floral/fleur-de-lis motifs.]

[A large historiated initial 'T' depicting a landscape with buildings and trees.]
HEODIDACT. Having surveyed and examined, with Cosmiel as guide and teacher, the highest habitations of the Heavens; having seen the nature, property, magnitude, and almost infinite multitude of the Celestial globes; having explored the ineffable fabric of the constitution of the entire superior world, at last, as if from a very deep sleep, I returned to myself—

the world

--- Page 26 ---
2                                 **Dialogue I.**

returned, I remained for a long time utterly astonished and dumbfounded at the dignity and excellence of the things I had seen; and my soul, now pregnant with desire for the eternal heights, with the utmost sweetness of mind, aspired to contemplate more closely those ineffable things it had seen; and in aspiring, it was carried away into immense transports of love for eternal Wisdom, the Architect of such great things. This one thing I implored from the fount of all Wisdom: that I might contemplate more closely the invisible things through those things which have been made, thus reasoning with myself: If divine goodness, by the sole guidance and leading of love, created such great and ineffable things in the vastness of this Universe for the use and preservation of rational creatures, how much more shall we deem it to have prepared her (the rational creature) in the insensible recess and abyss of its infinite essence, incomprehensible to man? Whose nature, dignity, and excellence, being indeed nearer and more similar to the divine essence, so much the more surpass all the beauty of corporeal and sensible things, as solar light far overcomes the densest fogs of darkness. And when at last, O Wisdom, Cos-
[Marginal note: Ardent de- / sire.] motechnitis, shall I be satisfied with your glory? When shall I be returned to you, from whom I flowed forth? When shall I be united to you, in whom all things are one? When shall I behold the Tri-une mirror of your divine essence? In which we shall contemplate both you and, together with you, all things, along with the fabric of the entire world and the symmetry of its individual parts? Oh, with what great abundance of delights, with what a torrent of pleasure shall we be filled and satisfied? When, absorbed in the ineffable abyss of your love, we shall be one with you through grace and the beatific vision,

--- Page 27 ---
**Cap.I. On the Nature of Water. 3**

...beatific, we who differ only by nature, shall we become? O God, what is there for me in heaven, and from you what have I desired on earth? God of my heart and my portion, God, forever, take, O take that which is like you, take my spirit marked with the character of your immortal essence; take my heart pledged to you by the ring of eternal love, break the chains of corruptible flesh, to sacrifice to you a victim of praise, dissolve the troublesome burden of the body, so that, established in the liberty of the children of God, I may possess you, love you, and be united to you in the center of eternal love, whose length, breadth, and depth, just as it has neither end nor number, so also, with its center existing everywhere, the circumference of its extension finds no limits anywhere.

Therefore, agitated by these and similar affections of my soul poured out into the incomprehensible majesty of Divine power, while at some unknown time I entered a certain suburban garden, I carefully observed the most beautiful order of trees arranged in a quincunx; the remarkable pleasantness of the groves, and especially the delightful dances of the leaping fountains, and the hidden origins of the gushing springs, wondering through which channels of veins such a mass of waters arranged its paths? how it was moved by such a perennial flow and never-interrupted motion? and from where, finally, it drew its immediate origin, I was burning with a great desire to know, and just as that pellucid clarity of the waters [pleased] the sight, so also the most pleasing sweetness [incited] the taste to investigate their nature,

--- Page 28 ---
4 Dialogue I.

[Marginal note: Ecstasy of Theodidactus.] dam, it stimulated me in a wonderful way; and so, while I commit my weary limbs to rest a little more softly on the most pleasant covering of the nearby grassy meadow, behold suddenly, seized by a certain heavy sleep, the playful spectacle of the fountains I had just been watching soon seemed to me to be transformed into a most elegant boy.
[Marginal note: Description of Hydriel.] The boy was somewhat plump and of a rather moist substance; in his right hand he carried a bucket, in his left a terrestrial globe; his eyes, mouth, nostrils, and budding ears seemed to drip drops of most limpid dew, and he addressed me with these words. Why are you tormented, Theodidactus? Why are you troubled on my account? Cease, cease, to be afflicted further, since with me as your instructor and guide you will attain perfect knowledge of those things which you so ardently desire to know. *Theodidactus*. And who are you, sweetest son? What is your name? Where do you come from? What do you imply with your words? Are you so skilled in natural things that you can instruct me, a man already advanced in age and graying, about the causes of such profound hidden things?
[Marginal note: Hydriel's offices.] *Boy*. I am called Hydriel and I bear the person of that great element which they call Water, and although I am a body devoid of all life, yet I bestow life upon all, lacking a soul, I animate all things; nay, by the command of my creator, I now present myself to you in the form of the living boy whom you behold, so that your questions concerning the works of divine Wisdom, which I will soon reveal to you, may be satisfied in every way.
[Marginal note: Explanation of symbols.] *Theodidactus*. And why do you present yourself to me in the form of a boy? *Hydriel*. Because I represent the element of water, which the rather moist substance of my body

--- Page 29 ---
Cap.I. On the Nature of Water. 5

my subsistence, and the drops of dripping dew diffused everywhere abundantly testify. But the bucket which I carry in my right hand, I signify by it the diffusion of waters into all paths of the terrestrial globe, which I carry in my left hand. But under the form of a boy, because the water which I represent always and perpetually seems to be born and reborn, continuously rejoicing, so to speak, with the joy of that youthful age. Now therefore proceed, propose those doubts which tormented your mind concerning my hidden nature, and I promise that I will resolve all things for you with a faithful answer. Theodidactus. Indeed, I fear too much lest perhaps you are one of that number of Daemons whom the ancients called Nymphs, and adored with sacrilegious worship as goddesses, which worship I execrate and abominate with every protestation of spirit I can, as a trick of evil spirits and a most wicked imposture. *Hydriel*. Do not be troubled, [Marginal note: Who Hydriel is.] Theodidactus, nor let any fear strike your mind, for I am by no means such as you, persuaded by false illusion, imagine me to be. For I am neither from the fabled chorus of Nymphs, nor any Lilith or Lamia, nor he whom the Poets call Neptune, but I am a pure and simple element, to which the name water belongs, and although I lack life, yet I praise and bless my creator in a manner suitable to my condition, as is permitted; also at his nod I tirelessly traverse all paths of the earth, both for the preservation of the world and for the use of the human race, for whose sake I was especially created; and I would not wish you to persuade yourself of anything other than what I have said, therefore only boldly-

--- Page 30 ---
6 **Dialogue I.**

only whatever things your soul desires concerning my nature, you examine in detail. *Theod.* Since therefore, led by I know not what internal sweetness of soul, I find the oracles of your voice most true, I will do what you command, and having invoked the name of the Triune God, I implore you, my Hydriel, that you explain to me your paths which you pursue. *Hydriel.* I will do what you ask very gladly; therefore, with attentive ears, listen to what I am about to narrate. Do you see this mountain placed opposite to you? *Theod.* [Marginal note: The paths of water are explained.] I see. *Hydr.* From it, on this very day, I first flowed forth. *Theod.* And what, I ask, is in that mountain that it can pour forth such deluges of water? *Hydr.* Know that in this mountain there is a huge reservoir of my element, or an aquatic storehouse, which from every side with unfailing diffusion, for the good of fields and plains, pours forth this abundance which you admire; therefore it cannot fail, because it has no end to its flow. *Theod.* But from where does that watery storehouse draw its origin? since it is established in the highest place; nor do I see how water can ascend there against nature, or how it can continue its course without a new, constant influx? *Hydr.* From the sea I draw my origin. *Theod.* [Marginal note: By what means water never fails in mountains.] How can this be, since the sea is very distant, and also much lower than this mountain? *Hydr.* Know, Theodidactus, that by the perpetual influence of the stars, I am agitated by ebb and flow on the widely open surface of the Ocean, whence it happens that, pressed by the violence and weight of the waves and floods, through hidden passages, by which the bottom of the Ocean no less,

--- Page 31 ---
**Cap. I. De Aquæ Natura . 7**

...no differently than a sieve, through which given opening I am forced to yield, and thus I open a path for myself through the winding and intricate meanders of the earth, until, having flowed out through it, I am finally restored, wandering over the outer surface of the earth, to the source from which I flowed. Theod. If you draw your origin from the sea, but the sea is imbued with saltiness by its nature, how have you abandoned your saltiness, since you are of the sweetest taste? Hydr. You must know, Theodidactus, that my saltiness is deposited partly by the clods of earth of sweet taste, which I pass through, and partly by the heat of the subterranean current, which in the gorges of the mountains is sometimes so great that I truly boil there as if in certain cauldrons placed over fires. With this boiling completed, as if cooked and digested, I lay aside all the bitterness of my native saltiness, and by this operation I offer a twofold use to the world: both a gushing of fresh water on the outer surface of the earth, and an internal economy for the incredible good of the earthly clods, where, in remuneration for the hospitality I have provided, I leave salt, without which the body of the earth could not possibly exist, as you will understand more fully from me later. But you must know that I do not have only one such channel by which I insinuate myself from the Ocean and seas into the innermost bowels of the earth, but truly innumerable ones in the bottom of the entire Ocean surrounding the earth, by which, no differently than blood is communicated through the ducts of veins in the human body to the entire Microcosm and to individual members for the sustenance of life, so too I extend myself through all my paths.

Theod. This is precisely what I have never been able to grasp at any time: therefore, tell me your ingenuity in such an ingenious play of nature.

Hydr. I told you above that the bottom of the sea is perforated by innumerable channels, by which my ocean diffuses itself into all the receptacles of the earth's interior, and I would like you to be persuaded that this diffusion occurs especially by this skill and ingenuity. Do you know those small channels which surgeons call syringes, which, filled with liquid, as soon as you insert the piston into them, the liquid contained therein is immediately ejected to a great height? From this shadowy resemblance of my operation, if I am not mistaken, you will easily understand the skill I commonly use in elevating myself above all things. Do you also know that my kingdom, the Ocean, is agitated by a perpetual reciprocation of tides, and that, according to the different position of the stars, the swelling of the waters increases or decreases more in one place and less in another? Consequently, it happens that from the flow of the Ocean, a mass of waters grows up like mountains, which mass of accumulated liquid, while by its own weight it [pushes] the liquid into the underlying...

10               Dialogue I.

where, placed perpendicularly, it presses with utmost force, so like a piston, with utmost vehemence, it urges the waters within the channels for discharge; but in the reflux of waters, certain truces are established with me, until I, through innumerable siphons of the earth, discharge myself into my workshops, into hidden, I say, water reservoirs, into the manifold ends of nature; and in this way, with the returning influx, by new and ever new agitation, I further my journeys towards the goal of the undertaking begun. And indeed, the same thing happens to me in this perpetual operation, which you, Theodidactus, [Marginal note: Experience with pumps.] see happening in pumps, of which one leg, while it presses the waters confined within the channel, causes a violent eruption of water from there, while with the other leg it prepares new waters for itself by its suction for expulsion; and thus this operation of mine is always in continuous and incessant motion, so arranged by the Creator's providence. Theod. Oh, how you captivate me with your ingenious reasoning, but I would like you to explain one more thing to me: and this is my doubt. If your influx should cease when the reflux supervenes, [Marginal note: Water-carrying channels are never deprived of water.] are not the water-carrying channels deprived of the necessary moisture? And if they are deprived of waters, how is it that we do not likewise see springs and rivers failing in their flow? Hydr. Know that my subterranean channels are perpetually filled with waters, so that from the bottom of the sea up to the very springs and rivers, I have a perpetual continuation with the sea; and the influx within the channels and the afflux within them is perennial and incessant. No differently than if someone from some lake water

--- Page 35 ---
**Cap. I. De Aquæ Natura. 11**

if someone has led water through lead pipes into some city, it is certain that water, just as it never fails in a lake, so by its continuous outflow, it never fails within the city's receptacles, arranged here and there by art. Nor, however, should you think that my channels are arranged like lead pipes; by no means: but through winding and rough paths they end in huge cauldrons hidden within the bowels of the mountains, of immense capacity, which, since they always contain an immense abundance of waters, it happens that through truces, the water between the channels not being disturbed, the cauldrons meanwhile full, continue the course of both springs and rivers through their discharge channels, until a little later they are refilled by a new influx of waters; moreover, when water is established between the channels, lest a vacuum intervene anywhere, one part draws the other, by a certain necessity of nature to preserve the unity and continuation of the flow. [Marginal note: Within the channels, water draws water by fear of a vacuum.]
*Theod.* I have rightly understood everything, and everything pleases me more than can be said; therefore I would now like you to explain to me how and by what means the Ocean can accomplish all these things. *Hydr.* The Ocean, as you know, first flows and ebbs four times in the space of almost twenty-four hours, by the efficacy of the benevolent moon, at whose most pleasing sight, as if of my kind nurse, I am soon, as if dancing and proud, raised with a great swelling, but when she departs, my pride laid aside, I am lowered: by my swelling, the channels are likewise urged to the ejection of my entrusted offspring, so by the depression, as if truces have been made, they cease from their violence, until again the [Marginal note: The ebb and flow of the Ocean is the purpose in the nature of things.]

...the moon rising, I burst forth into new revelries of swelling. And this struggle is so perpetual, so continuous, that there is scarcely the smallest space of time in which I am not reduced to similar straits somewhere in my Ocean kingdom, pressed by such ferocity of tumultuous waves, that no usual ejection between the channels is performed with greater force. Thus, even from this source, you may also recognize the perennial nature of my flow between the channels. Thirdly, there are winds, whether

[Marginal note:]
Winds swell the sea, both internal and external.

caused by external dispositions of the air, or by exhalations emerging outside my kingdom, or by subterranean spirits, it matters not: this one thing I say, that they (the winds) can do very much by the immense accumulation of waves, to agitate the waters situated within the channels. Then also, I am lifted up into the deep from the cauldrons of my nature through hidden channels ingeniously established by nature, by a certain attraction occurring from the fear of a vacuum; lifted up, through whatever open gate, I rush into springs and rivers. And agitated night and day by these three adversaries, yet ordered for the good of nature, I am perpetually moved in the channels of subterranean passages. Therefore, here you have in a few words the desired cause, how waters emerge from my Ocean kingdom, and through the windings of hidden paths...

**Chapter I. On the Nature of Water. 13**

*Theod.* It is clear to me from hydrostatic principles, and [Marginal note: Theodidactus's Objection.]
from the structure of pumps, that waters enclosed within channels
can by no means be pressed, unless the pressing force or weight
is greater, and heavier than the mass of water
it presses. Now no small doubt arises, whether
the impending weight of waters in the Ocean and its annexed seas
is sufficient to overcome such a mass of water enclosed
within the channels, since the channels in turn extend
through immense intervals of land. *Hydr.* You have judged correctly, Theodidactus, and so
it is; hence my provident mother, the nature of things,
willed the mouths of the channels at the bottom of the Ocean to be very wide,
but the remaining passages of the channels to be narrower,
almost in the form of a flexible pipe, so that the immense mass of agitated waters
superincumbent upon them might impart a more vehement impulse
to the waters enclosed within the channels;
for otherwise, if it were to happen, nature would labor in vain, if it did not
overcome by weight the waters it ought to propel: for all the works of God are
in number, weight, and measure, arranged by an ineffable
providence in such a way that one thing being posited, another
necessarily follows its effect. If it were given to you, Theodidactus, to see the
vastness of the abysses at the bottom of the sea, or also the
greatness of the passages which have a lateral entrance within the subterranean walls
of terrestrial regions and and continents, and the impulse of the entire sea
driven within them, as well as the force and efficacy of the weight of the deepest
waters incumbent upon them, by which under- [Marginal note: On the wonderful constitution of the channels.]

14 **Dialogus I.**

by which it presses the subterranean waters, perhaps you would have no doubt about the magnitude and multitude of such wonders. For just as the hidden secrets of my nature are concealed, and its paths inaccessible to mortals, so they are not easily open to human understanding, and are scarcely even penetrated by natural philosophers, however great their genius, so few are able to reach such a mystery of nature, and perhaps only those whom God has deemed worthy of the knowledge of such things by a special prerogative. *Theod.* I have understood enough and more than enough of what you wisely related, and now I no longer doubt the truth of the matter, therefore let us proceed to other things.
[Marginal note: Whence such a variety of color, taste, and odor in waters.]
Tell me, I ask, whence comes such a variety of colors, tastes, and odors in the water, with which you affect our senses? For sometimes you pour forth salty, then sweet, now warm, mostly cold, sometimes austere, sometimes imbued with a different odor, sometimes wholesome and suitable for healing various infirmities, nor are there lacking those which possess a certain pestilential and poisonous quality, which differences in qualities fill all investigators of nature with no small admiration.
[Marginal note: Solution to the questions made.]
*Hydr.* You should know, Theodidactus, that all these things depend on the natural constitution of the terrestrial parts through which my channels extend, for you should not think that the body of the earth's interior is homogeneous, for to think this, besides being characteristic of an insensate and ignorant philosophaster, even the external constitution of the earth itself, pregnant with such a variety of things, sufficiently and abundantly

**Cap. I. On the Nature of Water. 15**

And which demonstrates. Since these things are so, now even at first glance, the reasons for the differing waters, which shine forth in my springs, are evident; for whenever my channels insinuate themselves through diverse branches into caverns filled with salt, vitriol or sulfur, bitumen, naphtha, antimony, mercury, arsenic, orpiment, and similar minerals, it is certain that the water will be tinctured with the quality of such a mineral, whose place is fertile by its native power; hence everywhere such a great variety of waters imbued with the virtue of the aforementioned salts and minerals is commonly observed; it happens, however, that sometimes I must pass through places filled with toxic and poisonous qualities, which occurs especially in caverns, where the confluence of antimony, sulfur, naphtha, arsenic, mercury, and other foreign salts and spurious spirits possessing violent and deadly power takes place; then water imbued with these, wherever it breaks forth, brings not only extreme destruction to humans and animals, but also deprives the place of every inhabitant due to the deadly mephitis. I will say nothing further, for if you have thoroughly understood what has been said, you will find no effect in my element so unusual and prodigious, whose immediate cause you cannot instantly assign; therefore, to the intelligent, few words are needed.

following is a list of the most important things to remember about the text:

*   **The text is a translation of a Latin text.** This means that the language and style may be somewhat formal or archaic.
*   **The text is a discussion of the nature of water.** The author is trying to explain why water has different qualities depending on where it is found.
*   **The author believes that water acquires its qualities from the minerals it comes into contact with.** This is a common belief in ancient and medieval science.
*   **The author also acknowledges that some places contain toxic and poisonous qualities.** This can make the water in those areas dangerous

    Certain [channels] and hidden vents of nature are distributed, both for always attracting new and new air, and for preparing a new mass of combustible material, by a certain necessity of nature, lest they fail in their operations. Wherever, therefore, such volcanic channels encounter my cauldrons or water-storage casks, it happens that just as the volcanic channels boil with immense and perpetual heat, so upon encountering my cauldrons, they perfectly heat the water, which, then warmed by this heat, is finally discharged through appropriate small channels onto the outer surface of the earth into the hot springs, leaving behind, within the earth's bowels, the mixtures of salt and sulfur with which they were laden, so that you may therefore seek no other cause for the hot springs besides the one stated.
*Theod.* Do not your cauldrons, in time, get consumed by the force of the fires?
*Hydr.* Never, for they are denser and harder than Marpesian rock, carved out by the great providence of nature, and each is equipped with necessary and numerous channels for drawing off the heat of the fires; nor would I want you to imagine such channels filled with immense flames of fire; by no means, [Marginal note: The constitution of the fire-conducting channels.] for these (flames) have their own appointed place in Vulcan's forges; but they are filled with the immense vehemence of heat and very hot exhalations, imbued with various mixtures of minerals, by which my brother air, enclosed within them, boils so intensely that it does not yield to the heat of a lit furnace; this heat, however, since it depends on the perennial operation of Vulcan's workshops,

Cap. I. On the Nature of Water. 27

...according to the appropriate nature of places, I produce all kinds of salts, gums, mineral juices, and whatever smells so much of the nature of flow or moisture; whole books would have to be written, if I wished to explain in this place the manner and reason by which I am mixed with each (thing); I, by the aid of sulfur and mercury, by my industry, refine antimony, marcasite, ochre, arsenic, and if any other mineral body of great importance remains, into those wonderful powers by which they are potent; and indeed, I contribute even to the coagulation of gold itself—beyond which nothing torments human hearts so much—so that meanwhile I may be silent about the innumerable variety of stones and marbles, to all of which I confer that diversity of colors which you admire, by my flowing and dyeing faculty; in a word, I become all things to all things; with red earth I redden, I green with green, I purple with purple, with golden (things) I am dyed with a golden color, with yellow (things) I yellow, and whatever matter, prepared for rock or marble or precious stone, I touch with my dye, I immediately render it illustrious with its native beauty of color. Behold my ingenious play in the nature of things.

...in rightly establishing and elaborating which, my industry exerts itself; and these are, first, indeed the very body of the earth; secondly, the genus of trees and herbs; thirdly, the variety of animals, both quadrupeds and winged, aquatic, and creeping. Regarding the first, do you not see me clothing, adorning, irrigating, and nourishing the entire surface of the earth with innumerable gushings of springs and rivers, as if with certain ducts of the Geocosmic blood veins, so that from this very fact you may gather that I reach all things with the subtle efficacy of my penetrative power, and that there is no place where I am lacking, or where I do not assist by the duty entrusted to me by eternal wisdom,
[Marginal note: Water nourishes all things.]
and if sometimes, the nature of places so demanding, I seem to be absent somewhere, as in sandy deserts, nevertheless I by no means abandon the boundaries of jurisdiction assigned to me, but what the vehemence of the solar heat has rendered scorched, languid, arid, and sapless, that I soon restore, refresh, and bring back to fruitfulness by the abundance of nocturnal dew into which I am resolved, and thus I am nowhere lacking in my duty, where I am always present, and ready to succor the necessity of all.
[Marginal note: The utility of water in vegetable nature.]
I come to the second, which is vegetable nature, by which I am so anxiously sought, so solicitously courted, that there is no plantlet so small, no shrublet so small, that does not attract me with every effort of nature, otherwise to be consumed by sudden aridity and lack of nourishment. And this is wonderful to say, that although there are innumerable species of plants and trees, most distinct in forms and specific properties, nevertheless each of them, by an inherent power, attracts [me] into

**Cap. I. De Aquæ Natura. 29**

...themselves and their own nature. And since I operate according to the nature and condition of the place, I first dispose the earthy clod to such and such a quality by my seminal virtue and briny faculty, which I always carry enveloped in my center; this, being disposed and mixed with me, germinates such and such, such plants and trees and no others; it produces them from a certain wonderful tempering and mixture of the earthy with the moist and other hidden qualities of the concurring places. From the adaptation of this infinite combination, that infinite variety of herbs and plants is born, which then, growing up by the propagation of conceived and excluded seed, fill the entire surface of the earth for the use of men and animals, whence the common proverb, *not every land bears everything*, since I cannot produce anything unique without the appropriate nature and condition of the soil concurring. Hence in India and the regions subject to the Torrid Zone, I produce plants and trees entirely different from European ones. And why is this? Because they obtain a different position relative to the Sun, Moon, and stars, by which, in different ways, both the virtues of the celestial influences and the Archaeus, ministers and architects of the subterranean Economy, participate in operations, so wonderfully also is the nature of the terrestrial parts altered by them. [Marginal note: According to the different constitution of the sky, diverse things are generated.] *Theod.* Oh, how skillfully and expertly you explain the nature of things. But now I desire to learn further from you, how you involve yourself in the generation and temperament of animals? *Hydr.* I will briefly show you the method, so that from it you may gather the admirable cycle of nature in all things. Every animal, whether it be of the order of those endowed with reason, or those lacking it, whether quadrupeds or birds, or whether they derive their origin from the family of aquatic creatures and insects—every animal, I say, needs nourishment to live. That nourishment is supplied either by the flesh of animals, or by the pasturage of herbs, fruits, vegetables, and legumes. All these derive their radical origin from me, as I demonstrated a little while ago, since without me they could by no means attain the perfection of their essence. I, with my very subtle and thin substance, first, do not so much enter the roots of plants, as I am attracted by them by some unknown hidden force of magnetism. To these I join the strength necessary for sustaining the plant. Then I am mixed with the substance of the plant itself, now enriched with peculiar powers. And in this way, rarefied by the external heat of the sun, I gradually burst forth from the earth, and with the always new and new increase of my nourishment succeeding, I am finally condensed, expanded, arranged, protruded, and animated into stem, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seed. The mature and already digested seed is again committed to the earth, so that, fermented by my work, it may rise into a new offspring of the plant, by a certain perennial cycle of nature's own propagation. indeed unsuitable for human habitation, yet so useful to the entire Geocosm that it cannot exist without them. You know the Ocean is agitated by a continuous ebb and flow, now from east to west, now from south

The Ocean, therefore, absorbed in the said whirlpool, which we said was located under the Arctic pole, rolling down its waters through the aforementioned channel, after filling the receptacles of a more secret Nature and the purification by decoction having been completed, is again regurgitated through the opening of the parts located under the Antarctic pole; for this is entirely similar to that opening of the whirlpool which exists under the Arctic, thus

*Cosmiel.* You should know, Theodidact, that the element of air differs little from water; since it is like the most subtle vapor or emanation of water, or as it were, a certain outflow of the same, which necessarily results when water is placed and heat dissolves it. For as I indicated to you above, as soon as this divine voice, "Let there be light," resounded, the element of fire, or primordial light, quickly rarefied the waters, expanded by its heat, into the most subtle substance, and this we call air or Aether. For as is clear to you from experience, it is very easy for water to be changed into air, and this in turn into water. Since therefore the Sacred Text says that fish and birds came forth from water, it implies that the former (fish) came from a thicker moisture, but the latter (birds) from a more subtle moisture, which is air.

For since the elements are so connected to each other by nature that one cannot exist without the other, and one is always the nourishment of the other, and all mutually cherish, animate, and preserve each other by such strict laws of friendship, that it would rather be necessary for the world to perish than for one to be deprived of the mutual aid of another. [Marginal note:]
How plants are generated.

This wonderful action of plant generation occurs in the following way. As soon as the aforementioned nourishment has been drawn in a sensible manner through the roots from the earth, and in an insensible manner through the pores of the plant from the air, it is immediately digested by the vegetative power of the plant soul through the spirits, and cooked in the innermost recess of its members; and when cooked and digested, it is converted into nourishing substance. And from its purer and more subtle part, seed is formed, which is preserved in a peculiar way in its small body for the generation and multiplication of plants. Indeed, this earthly deposit is dissolved into its primary matter, from which it was formed, through that nourishing moisture infused with the nectar-like liquid of celestial light; and thus dissolved, it sprouts and germinates, and blossoms into a plant similar to itself.

# Genesis of Birds.

[Marginal note:]
Twofold nourishment

**C**OSMIEL. Every kind of bird is born from seed, seed from nourishment, and nourishment indeed draws its primary origin partly from the insensible air, and partly from the sensible nourishment on which they feed. The insensible nourishment indeed is air, imbued with the virtue of celestial seed, which they can by no means lack without loss of life. Their sensible nourishment, however, consists of all those things on which birds are accustomed to feed. From both these, the hidden and the manifest, the sensible and the insensible nourishment, joined together, the seed of birds is born. This seed, brought into actuality, propagates into an innumerable multitude and variety, filling the entire lowest region of the air, so that they may inhabit the element from which they originated. Therefore, all elements converge for the composition of birds, no differently than in mixed bodies, which are mixed into one general seed of nature, individualized according to the disposition of the subject matter. And just as a form is constituted for each by the active virtue of celestial light or seed, so too from the same, according to the individualized light's relation in distinct matter, various powers and properties of birds have emanated as if from a source. And just as from air and water the seed of both contributes to the constitution of birds, so that [seed] hidden in water alone contributes to the generation of fish, and mixed in earth and water to the production of quadrupeds and plants, with water flowing together in the production of all living things, and even minerals, as a certain passive universal principle of all things, since without it no element can attain its desired effect, nor can fire, earth, or air exist in any way without it; for it is the nourishment of all, the bearer of all other elements, by whose aid all the treasures of the world, together with the seeds of heaven and the elements, are transported into the subterranean storehouses of nature, there to be digested and diffused into every circumference; so that it is no wonder that such a great and innumerable [quantity], as we see in no other element,

Dialogus II.

Genesis Insectorum.

[Threefold kind
of insects.]
COSMIEL. It must be noted that, taking this name "insects" a little more broadly for our purpose, there are three kinds. For one kind contains flying insects, another creeping insects, another multi-legged insects, which again are divided into various and different species. The first kind comprises flies, gall wasps, bruchus beetles, scarabs, locusts, butterflies, of which there is no number. The second kind (comprises) all genera of serpents and worms. The third embraces animals equipped with both four and many feet; such as shrews, mice, lizards, crocodiles, and whatever finally, partly from putrefaction, partly from the mixing of its own seed, multiplies into infinite progeny. Multi-legged creatures contain all genera and species of spiders, lice, bedbugs, caterpillars, and crustacean worms, which indeed have their origin from the putrefaction of mixtures, or are born from plants, or from animals, or from the putrid refuse of terrestrial matter which has flowed together in air, water, earth: and in this manner they are animated.

[How insects
are born from
putrefaction.]
For since putrefaction is nothing other than a confluence of undigested humor, whether it occurs in plants, or in animals, or in any mixture of elements, which, just as it is potent with richness and heat, so the primordial light or seed of the world, undivided in that matter, suddenly by its internal heat, on account of proximate

So much so, that there is no plant, no animal, no element which does not, except fire, produce some insect. And this is also to be noted, that no mixture in the world can produce any insect unless it first had life, whence only metallic and mineral bodies, as they are not subject to any putrefaction, so also they generate no insect animals. But if any worms are sometimes found in the pores of stones, this does not arise from the fact that they were immediately generated from the rock, but because seed was carried into the pores of the rock from elsewhere, from which the worms flowed forth; all of which, since you have shown more fully in your works, I do not wish to be longer here.

I will describe to you a shadowy likeness of it, but first I shall have laid a deeper foundation for a subject so replete with profound contemplations.
      The Most Holy and Indivisible Trinity, God, Best and Greatest, when from eternity, hidden in the darkness of His inaccessible light, in the archetype of divine Ideas, He contemplated Himself with the infinite complacency of His own beatitude, most sufficient unto Himself, impelled by an incomprehensible and ineffable instinct of goodness, and by infinite love, so that He might bring forth into visible light the efficacy of His omnipotence, lying hidden within the center of His Divine essence, it pleased Him to produce this corporeal world, according to the eternal exemplars of ideal notions, so that, indeed, outside the immensity of His divine essence, [Marginal note: The world created for man.] a creature endowed with intellect might be produced, which might behold the great works of God's omnipotent power, that is, the invisible things, through those things which have been made. So that He who was invisible in Himself, might nevertheless appear visible in such a great work of the world, so perfect, adorned with such a variety of things, administered with such order, as if in so many mirrors of His divinity, which are the posteriora Dei. Therefore, the world having been constituted in this manner, [Marginal note: Angels co-created.] He first created the angelic nature, most similar to Himself in image above all creatures, both as admirers of His glory and as guardians of the work produced by Him. Amen. *Cosmiel.* But now it is time for me to return to the administration of the world committed to me. *Theod.* O Cosmiel, Cosmiel, if I have found favor in your eyes, take my soul, so that, with the troublesome burden of this body removed, I may dwell with you in the eternal courts of blessedness. For your departure seems to me harder than death itself. *Cosmiel.* Did I not tell you that your will must be conformed in all things to the Divine? Have you so suddenly forgotten my words? First carry out the doctrine delivered to you here, so that, full of the accumulation of merits, you may at last attain your end. *Theod.* Therefore, let the will of God be fulfilled in all things, but this one thing I ask of you: that you do not abandon your servant in the future, but always assist me in all necessities, so that at last I may enjoy your sweet, and more delightful than can be conceived, companionship in the homeland. *Cosmiel.* Do not doubt, son, I will always assist you, I will protect you, I will help you in all your works, as you have asked. *Theod.* But oh, in what ways, oh sweetest Cosmiel; oh Master of Divine Wisdom, shall I repay the grace for your innumerable benefits bestowed upon me? With what weight of words, with what gravity of arguments, shall I explain your ineffable kindness towards me to the world? *Cosmiel.* To God in me, and through me, whatever good things you have obtai-

--- Page 251 ---
Cap. V. Ascetic Epilogue. 227

whatever good things have fallen to your lot, let it suffice to have ascribed that. Peace be with you, my beloved Theodidactus, die to the world, live to God, always mindful of me and my words. Farewell. Theod.
With these words, he immediately vanished into thin air. But I, as if waking from a very deep sleep, found myself entirely covered in sweat, which was accompanied by the greatest weakness of all my limbs; until, a little while refreshed, I felt my former strength restored to me. Therefore, nothing more remains, but that whatever things are contained in this Journey may redound solely to the glory of God and the salvation of one's neighbor.

# SYNOPSIS
### Of those things which are extensively discussed
### in ten Books in the Work of the Subterranean
### World.

[Decorative initial P depicting a landscape with figures] RESENTING a PROLOGUE without written witnesses of its undertaking seemed entirely unfitting; Therefore, I decided that this present Synopsis should be appended, by which the entire subject of the Subterranean World might be displayed to the curious Reader; driven especially by this reason, that several people had long since requested it from me; while they could not grasp what exactly could be in the subterranean recess of the Terrestrial globe, which either deserved the name of a World, or which could furnish arguments worthy of the name of a World; indeed deluded by a false and common persuasion, who, just as they think the terrestrial globe is compacted by a fortuitous conglomeration no differently than a curd of cheese, so far are they from persuading themselves that, besides certain crypts and mines near the terrestrial surface, other receptacles are constituted within, that rather they firmly believe, not without a certain obstinacy of mind, that everything is packed with immense solidity. Therefore, so that such a palpable error might be removed from those ignorant of these matters, it seemed good to set forth in this place before the eyes of the curious Reader the whole series of our undertaking;
from

--- Page 253 ---
229

From which it will indeed be clearly evident that no effects so unusual appear in this sensible World that they are not found, according to a certain analogy, in the innermost bowels of the earth; and that, moreover, the origins of all things derive their origin solely from the Subterranean World.
But with these premises, let us now set forth the sequence of matters to be discussed and the division of the work.

are the Stars themselves; The Workshop, the Archetypal Mind; The Printer, is the Triune G O D. Who presents this book to you to be read, by day as if on the brightest pages of innumerable variety of things, by night, indeed on black ones, but inscribed with golden letters, that is, wonderfully conspicuous with the radiant mantle of the stars. Man is the index and summary of the book: the censor and approver was He, who saw that all things which He had made were very good. In this Journey the sacred mysteries of the celestial book will be explained to you, so that you may behold with the freest impulse of your mind, how many crowns for the crown of an earthly point, how many kingdoms for kingdoms, how ample, how spacious G O D, the Best and Greatest, has prepared in the recesses of the higher world. 2                                     Preface

...that it might bring prevaricators to their senses. Which, just as formerly, so also especially in these last centuries, happened to the great astonishment of mortals. Venerable antiquity had never known anything about the existence of a New World in the nature of things, nothing about the vast diffusion of the Ocean around the globe of lands; nothing had it discovered about the state of the Antipodes; but behold, God, the Best and Greatest, after the times of His inscrutable counsel were fulfilled, opened for us a new theater of the World, filled with such a variety of exotic things as we read with admiration from the records of the historians of the New World; which, if anyone had recounted to the Ancients, they would undoubtedly have judged them, I will not say among probable histories, but as pure and utter fables and old wives' tales. This display of divine benevolence did not stop here, when, not so long an interval of years after the discovery of the New World, He expanded for us a new theater of Celestial spectacles, and revealed things unheard of in all preceding centuries by the benefit of the celestial tube. The structure of the mundane machine, from time immemorial until now, had shown only the external beauty of its face to humans, but now, with the shell opened, it revealed the kernel, and with the enclosures opened, the interior state of things, the position, arrangement, and proportion of the wheels, also the composition of the globes, the functions of the centers, and the matter and form by which each thing is composed...

--- Page 285 ---
                  To the Reader.                  3
composed; it reveals the hidden paths of motions, unfolded the nests of light and heat to the great astonishment of philosophers, so that there was scarcely anyone who did not run with armed eyes to contemplate with utmost effort the unusual wonders of nature. Here, onto the stage of the heavens, came forth, besides ancient things (but formerly indistinct in nebulous stars), and throughout the entire circuit of the Galaxy, throngs of numerous stars; the origins of new stars in Cassiopeia, Ophiuchus, and Cygnus, wonderfully differing in nature, property, figure, and diversity of colors; so that I may meanwhile omit the variety of Comets, dire omens for mortals. Here the Sun, than which the world hitherto believed nothing brighter or more splendid, transformed by a certain wonderful variety of spots and shadows, and as if producing immense ebullitions of heat, appeared as the most constant star of the World, subject to a perpetual vicissitude of alterations. Here the Moon, burdened with mountains, lakes, seas, islands, presented itself on the stage; which Venus followed, with a horned forehead, not so beautiful due to the roughness of its parts

--- Page 286 ---
**4 Preface**

Jupiter's planet, surrounded by four splendors, not so much of satellites as of princely bodies, rarely girded transversely by a single belt, more often by a double, more rarely by a triple; finally, Saturn closes the procession, the Geryon of the Planets, admirable for the wonder and astonishment of its three-bodied star, exhibited itself in a form awe-inspiring to behold. Therefore, this new arrangement of the World and the unheard-of luxuriant fertility of nature, although it attracted the eyes of all astronomers to itself, yet it can hardly be said how much the causes of such unusual effects have strained the intellect of every single person. And just as rumors of unusual things wonderfully stir everyone's ears, so it anxiously stimulated not only the curiosity of mathematicians and philosophers, but also that of princes. Among these, the Most August Emperor Ferdinand III can deservedly be counted, a most munificent Maecenas, who, by a praiseworthy instinct of his curiosity, while urging the secret mysteries of the subterranean world, long since begun by me, also ordered the reasons and causes of such celestial wonders, which the sagacity of this age has brought forth, to be explained together; indeed, thinking it a sin not to obey his command, I composed this new little work, extracted not so much by spontaneous effort as by the insistent entreaty of so great a Prince and others; which indeed, so that it might more pleasantly and agreeably into the minds of readers

--- Page 287 ---
**To the Reader.** 5

...which indeed, so that it might flow more pleasantly and agreeably into the minds of readers, it was decided to arrange it in the form of a dialogue, designated by the name of the Ecstatic Journey, in which, recalling to the anvil the collection of observations made up to this point, I intended, with intense mental contemplation, persistent study, and investigation of various combinations of things, as well as with a manifold apparatus of things, to unravel the hidden causes of so many paradoxes from the inaccessible darkness in which they were enveloped up to these times, and by assigning reasons, to demonstrate that the fabric of the World was constituted by principles much more recondite than either the simplicity of past ages or the common philosophers of this time could persuade themselves of; and to teach that much greater things lie hidden in those hidden confines and repositories of a higher nature than has hitherto been believed, to be revealed someday in their own times for the solace of mortals. Before I do this, I wished to protest here with that ingenuousness and candor of mind which is fitting, that I would bring nothing into this little work, [Author's Protestation.] unless it is everywhere consistent with the Holy Fathers, Sacred Scripture, and experiments deduced from observations. But when the Reader has perhaps unfolded the bolder conversations of Theodidactus with Cosmiel, when he has silently considered raptures, ecstasies, and exotic operations, and similar affections and effects of contemplatives, I earnestly ask this of him.

--- Page 288 ---
6                   Preface

I earnestly implore him not to allow the shadow of some sinister suspicion, I know not what, to settle in his mind concerning me;
and therefore accuse me of some rashness, as if I were arrogating to myself something higher than human, or as an oracle of revelations divinely inspired in me, a new prophet, I were attempting to push forth a new apocalypse into the world with too much confidence, or as if I wished to claim for myself more than is right, that I had been privy to the secret counsel of the Divine Power: far be it! For how much the ambition of such mischievous men is abhorrent to my soul, those know who know me and all that is mine. Therefore, the end and sole intention of the undertaken Work was to follow that method in this little book which long ago among the ancients, Trismegistus, Plato, Lucian, and in succeeding ages many poets and orators, indeed, laudably maintained by custom; a method, I say, which a pleasant, delightful, and to the Reader's taste accommodated style of speaking would adorn, while the allegorical coverings of the narratives would gently temper the shadowy lines of the drawings, as it were, with light and color, and also the Thaumaturgic operations described in poetic style, stimulating the Reader's mind with a certain curiosity, would carry it away with a gentler impulse to the consideration of the proposed matters; therefore, here is no mystery, no rapture or of divine Power

Here's a breakdown of the Latin text and its translation, with explanations where needed:

**Ad Lectorem.**
*   **Ad:** To (accusative, indicating direction/recipient).
*   **Lectorem:** Reader (accusative singular of *lector*).
*   **Translation:** To the Reader.

**reu elationem, nullam epiphaniam angelicam; nul-**
*   **revelationem:** Revelation (accusative singular of *revelatio*).
*   **nullam:** No, none (accusative singular feminine, agreeing with *epiphaniam*).
*   **epiphaniam angelicam:** Angelic epiphany (accusative singular feminine).
*   **Translation:** revelation, no angelic epiphany; no

**lum Oraculi Delphici afflatum subesse velim; sed**
*   **lum:** (part of *nullum*) no, none (accusative singular masculine, agreeing with *afflatum*).
*   **Oraculi Delphici:** Of the Delphic Oracle (genitive singular).
*   **afflatum:** Inspiration, divine breath (accusative singular of *afflatus*).
*   **subesse:** To be present, to underlie (infinitive, dependent on *velim*).
*   **velim:** I would wish (present subjunctive of *volo*).
*   **sed:** But.
*   **Translation:** Delphic Oracle's inspiration to underlie it, I would wish; but

**ut omnia luculenter demonstrentur, ratiocinia-**
*   **ut:** So that, in order that.
*   **omnia:** All things (neuter plural nominative/accusative).
*   **luculenter:** Clearly, lucidly (adverb).
*   **demonstrentur:** May be demonstrated (present subjunctive passive, 3rd plural).
*   **ratiociniaque:** And reasonings, and arguments (*ratiocinia* is neuter plural nominative/accusative, *que* is "and").
*   **Translation:** that all things may be clearly demonstrated, and that reasonings

**que de rebus adeo incognitis suauius Lectoris ani-**
*   **de rebus:** About things (ablative plural).
*   **adeo:** So, to such an extent.
*   **incognitis:** Unknown (ablative plural, agreeing with *rebus*).
*   **suavius:** More pleasantly, more gently (comparative adverb).
*   **Lectoris animo:** To the reader's mind/soul (dative singular).
*   **Translation:** about things so unknown might be more pleasantly instilled in the Reader's mind,

**mo ingererentur, sub ingeniosi figmẽti velamine seu**
*   **ingererentur:** Might be instilled, might be introduced (imperfect subjunctive passive, 3rd plural).
*   **sub:** Under (preposition with ablative).
*   **ingeniosi figmenti:** Of an ingenious fiction/device (genitive singular). *Figmenti* is a variant of *figmenti*.
*   **velamine:** Veil, covering (ablative singular).
*   **seu:** Or.
*   **Translation:** under the veil of an ingenious fiction or

**ficti raptus integumento exhibita esse Lector sibi**
*   **ficti raptus:** Of a feigned rapture/ecstasy (genitive singular).
*   **integumento:** Covering, cloak (ablative singular).
*   **exhibita esse:** To have been presented/shown (perfect infinitive passive).
*   **Lector:** Reader (nominative singular).
*   **sibi:** To himself (dative reflexive pronoun).
*   **Translation:** under the covering of a feigned rapture, the Reader should persuade himself that these things have been presented;

**persuadeat velim; Ne verò solus intellectus mi-**
*   **persuadeat:** May persuade (present subjunctive, 3rd singular).
*   **velim:** I would wish (present subjunctive of *volo*).
*   **Ne verò:** Lest indeed, so that not truly.
*   **solus intellectus:** The intellect alone (nominative singular).
*   **mi-:** (part of *mirandorum*) of wonderful.
*   **Translation:** I would wish him to persuade himself; Lest indeed the intellect alone,

**randorum operum magnitudine captus sine ulla**
*   **randorum operum:** Of wonderful works (genitive plural).

revelation, no angelic epiphany; no
Delphic Oracle's inspiration to underlie it, I would wish; but
that all things may be clearly demonstrated, and that reasonings
about things so unknown might be more pleasantly instilled in the Reader's mind,
I would wish the Reader to persuade himself that these things have been presented under the veil of an ingenious fiction or
