hence, in the manner of ascetics, the Theodidactus (one taught by God),
after the greatest works of the most wise Creator, rapt into acts of divine love, and into affections of admiration,
intends nothing else than to incite the Reader to similar thanksgivings due to God,
to similar affections of a soul full of God, so that in this way,
through the visible wonders of this worldly machine, he may aspire to the abundance of invisible goods that never
fail, seek them with the whole affection of his mind, and finally,
in the eternal fellowship of the sons of God, and possessed of eternal happiness, may rest in Him
who is the ultimate end, eternal blessedness, and
the center of all creation. Therefore, these things having been pre-
mised, let us now at last pursue the argument of the matter proposed to us.

# PRELUDE
# HORTATORY,

*In which the Author clearly teaches that this little work*
*contains nothing foreign that does not agree with the*
*authorities of the Sacred Scriptures and the Doctors*
*of the Holy Church, and with irrefutable experiments*
*of observations.*

[Decorative initial I]n preparing an ecstatic Itinerary, I have deemed it necessary to first reveal my mind to the curious Reader concerning some things absolutely necessary to know, so that in this way the Reader might traverse the path to the celestial regions, which is to be opened by us, with hoped-for fruit, and the hidden paths of higher nature with an unhindered foot.

Many things, I confess, occur in it which might deservedly seem entirely new, paradoxical, and hitherto unheard of to one inexperienced in nature; yet these are so far from being such, that rather nothing so unusual and wonderful occurs in this entire reasoning of ours, which does not in large part agree-

--- Page 291 ---
agrees. To demonstrate this, four things must be proven by me in this Itinerary, which if, as I hope, are rightly and sincerely assessed, free from all pretense and disturbance of ill will, I am confident that I will certainly obtain complete belief in the truth shining forth in the creation of the world and the structure of celestial bodies.

First, that in the celestial World, with the exception of the stellar bodies, no other solidity is admitted or can or ought to be admitted, and therefore the entire heaven, from the uppermost region of the air up to the Empyrean heaven, is liquid and ethereal. Second, that there is no body in the nature of things which is not subject to alterations and corruptions at least in part, and therefore all the spherical bodies of the stars are subject to these laws of alteration by a certain necessity of nature, inasmuch as they cannot subsist without them, and that heaven itself, with all its bodies, is corruptible. Third, that all the starry bodies of the World are composed of a mixture of the four elements in a manner suitable to them, no less than the earth, differing only in properties and qualities, and that each was also furnished with its own proper centers by the supreme Creator of the World. Fourth, that according to a certain analogy, all bodies of the World bear the same relation to each other as the Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, and Earth bear to each other. These points I could indeed extensively prove here with the aforementioned authorities, were it not that distinguished men, P. Johannes Baptista Ricciolius in his *Almagestum Novum*, and P. Christopher B Schei-

--- Page 292 ---
10           Prelude

Our Scheiner, in his *Rosa Ursina*, from folio 591 to 784, had demonstrated [these points]: where, with the greatest and incredible diligence, he not only amassed sacred authorities drawn from the founts of divine oracles for the liquid nature of the heavens and for the fiery and watery substance of the stars, against the imperishability or incorruptibility of the heavens and stars, but also so strengthened these arguments by copiously adducing testimonies of almost all the Holy Fathers and their genuine interpretations, and expounded them so solidly, learnedly, and skillfully by reason, and by experience, the guiding mistress of all, with the unanimous consent of all agreeing astronomers, that concerning the truth of such great authorities, the weight of the adduced reasons, and the irrefutable certainty of observations performed by astronomers throughout the whole world, it cannot be doubted any further in the future; and the Reader will openly discover that I bring forward nothing in this entire Itinerary that they have not previously asserted as proven from innumerable authors.

The Reader will also find in the said work of Scheiner, that besides the fiery and watery nature of the stars and the liquidity of the heavens, all bodies of the world, being composed of the four elements, are thus subject to generations and corruptions; and where he discusses the origin of comets and new stars, he teaches extensively that these things exist: here (he teaches) that individual globes of astral bodies exhale their own atmospheres, that individual ones are equipped with their own centers, and that individual ones possess different modes of influence. ...nature; but you will discover the Moon, on the contrary, obscured by humidity, and the revolution of the stars around their own center. Following him were Reita and Wendelinus, who, supported by their own experience and the aid of a celestial eye, the former in his 'Eye of Enoch and Elijah', the latter in various Astronomical treatises, so proved it, that anyone wishing to maintain the contrary opinion would have to be considered, not a genius, but rather a philosopher of a stubborn mind. If therefore the Holy Fathers, by the light of reason alone drawn from sacred sources, proved the liquid and corruptible nature of the heavens with such a weight of arguments, and tried with such earnestness to persuade others; what, if they had been instructed by the observations of this time, shall we think they would not have achieved? Certainly, Scheinerus, Mersennus, and others extensively prove that Aristotle alone was the first among all philosophers of past centuries who asserted the solidity of the heavens, confused the world with intricate coverings of orbs, and introduced a fifth essence incomprehensible to any intellect; to therefore believe that heathen Sophist more, and to value his authority more than that of the Holy Fathers, they consider to be, if not unjust, at least rash.

    Therefore, having examined both the sources of Sacred Scripture concerning celestial discipline, and the most learned explanations of the Holy Fathers on Genesis and other passages of the sacred text relevant to this matter; and also having combined with these the wonderful observations of the most acute Philosophers and Astronomers of this time—
                                B  2                               observations,

I have used this reasoning, however: if the heaven or firmament is liquid, as the Holy Fathers explain from the sacred scriptures, then the heaven exists as one and threefold, everywhere permeable, everywhere penetrable, placing no impediments or obstacles whatsoever to the astral bodies moving within it; one in respect to its continuous liquidity, threefold in respect to the difference of its regions; and these are the aerial, sidereal, and empyrean heavens, to which they say Saint Paul was raptured; which, however, as it is far removed beyond all terms of natural constitution, so it is reached by faith alone. They differ from one another only by the diversity of forms and properties; just as in the terrestrial globe, in which, even if innumerable species of things are found to differ in forms and properties, nevertheless all things are found to be the same as regards elementary matter, as is clear from chemical analysis; but this more fully in our Itinerary. Therefore let no one wonder if we assert that celestial globes of solar nature are formed from liquid fire and an earthly portion, but those of lunar nature from water and earthly substance; for these things are deduced by natural consequence from the presuppositions. For what is to be considered to happen in the terrestrial globe, let us likewise suppose that to happen in celestial bodies according to a certain analogy, so that whatever actions follow the conjunction of elements, those same actions can certainly be inferred to be found in celestial globes, more in one, less in another; therefore, besides the primary qualities, there also exist secondary ones in celestial globes: lightness, gravity, softness, hardness, rarefaction, condensation; from which, in their own way, meteorological impressions conforming to them necessarily follow; therefore, all things which are observed in the terrestrial globe must necessarily also be observed in the celestial ones, if you except the vegetable and sensitive nature, which the reason of eternal wisdom has excluded therefrom; Hence, just as on Earth, as St. Dionysius testifies, individual species of things have a presiding Angel, so also do the individual elements of the celestial globes [have Angels], who direct them to their ends, intended by nature, the minister of God,

...and impenetrable recesses, they differ by an inexplicable distance; so that, accordingly, some philosophers of this time are less to be approved, who not only abstain from experiments and observations, but are accustomed to greatly abhor them; lest, led by sense and reason, they be compelled to depart even a little from the ancient Peripatetic opinions, or to add anything to their prescribed tenets, or to change anything in them. Moreover, whoever desires to know the contemporary novelties concerning the doctrine of celestial phenomena, let him consult first Scheiner in the cited book, then the most learned and most erudite Father Giovanni Battista Riccioli's New Almagest, book 8 and 9, where he treated, with keen care and incredible diligence, whatever can be conceived concerning this doctrine; where he will also find the names of all authors who either discovered new things in the heavens, or from these discoveries attempted to establish a new philosophy, truly the most abundant storehouse of the entire astronomical discipline.

And since there is a remarkable diversity of opinions concerning the reasons and causes of celestial phenomena, what we think from the presupposed foundations, and how all, even paradoxes, can everywhere be defended with the greatest ease, having followed a certain middle path, we have decided to demonstrate in this Ecstatic Journey. If the fair reader, having laid aside all biased affection, shall have weighed these things in the equal balance of truth, and shall have duly discussed the reasons adduced, he will undoubtedly, besides the easiest solution to all difficulties which up to this

--- Page 310 ---
28      Prelude

...which up to this time have tormented almost all schools. He will confess the solution, after each point has been duly explored according to the rules of the combinatorial art, that the creation of the World cannot be otherwise than we have said. But if anyone should bring forward something better than our reasons, we promise that we will not be unwilling to subscribe to it. But lest we assert anything contrary to the decrees and institutions of the Holy Roman Church, we contend for this one thing: that we should perpetually proscribe the inhabitants of the celestial globes along with the mobility of the earth. But if anything suspicious, either through inadvertence or inattention, should have burst forth against my intention, I wish it to be revoked and retracted by these words.

However, so that each point might flow into the minds of readers with greater delight, we have arranged this little work in the form of a Dialogue, with Cosmiel and Theodidactus as interlocutors; in which, under the guise of an ecstasy or rapture, various difficulties of doubts arising concerning the reasons for the celestial globes are resolved back and forth through reciprocal questions and answers, according to the knowledge of observations made. And this is for the greater pleasure of the readers; and for the relaxation of the minds of Princes, weary with the cares of political affairs, who urgently requested this very thing from me. But so that some spiritual benefit might thence be brought to minds devoted to God, physical contemplations, mostly ardent, receive affections of admiration and love for God, the Creator of such great things. And lest anything should be lacking in this little work concerning the constitution of the World, in the second part we intend to treat of divine providence...

CHAPTER I.
On the cause and origin of this Little Work.

[Large decorative initial V]UST as I have always had a most ardent
desire for knowing things that have hitherto remained hidden, so too, and most especially, my heart has burned with eagerness to penetrate this admirable world-machine and to investigate the extraordinary things which God, Best and Greatest, whose wisdom is without number or end, has placed in that supreme dwelling of the heavens; especially in these times, when the supreme and infinite goodness of God has somewhat [opened] His theater to men
Astro-

--- Page 313 ---
**of this little work. 31**

nomers dedicated to the study of Astronomy, by the aid of the astronomical tube, He opened up things truly wonderful and unheard of in previous centuries, which I myself would never have believed, had I not explored them with my own eyes with the greatest joy of my soul, and learned them through continuous communication with all the best astronomers of this age.
But what indeed was that in the mountainous Moon, diffused as it were into certain lakes? What indeed was that in the Sun, boiling like a fiery ocean, and shining with spots and torches? What in Venus and Mercury, crescent-shaped in the manner of the Moon? What it was in Mars, exhaling I know not what smoky matter, it was not permitted to penetrate; I admired the splendor and supreme Majesty of Jupiter, surrounded by such an unusual retinue of satellites; I considered Saturn's sphere and its wonderful structure, and I was struck with awe; having explored the secrets of the firmament, I was astounded; but what indeed all those things were, I was at a loss, and I grieved greatly, that God, the Best and Greatest, had given this affliction to the sons of men; so that man may not find the work which God has wrought from the beginning even to the end; I groaned at that (saying) of Ecclesiasticus, that many things are hidden, greater than these which we know and understand, and that we see few of the works of God. That (saying) of Sirach deterred me, "Do not labor, for you will not comprehend them;" on the contrary, that (saying) encouraged me: "Has not the Lord caused the Saints to declare all His wonders, which the Almighty has confirmed to establish in His glory," and the benevolent invitation of the Father of lights; "Come and see the works of the Lord and the wonders which the Lord has wrought above in heaven, and below on earth." Stirred by these things, I said in my heart:

CHAPTER II.

§. I.

An Ecstatic Journey to the Moon.
Theodidactus.

[Marginal note: Michael Angelus Rossius. Lalius Chorista. Salvator Mazzella.]
It happened not long ago, that I was invited to an academic
exercise of three incomparable Musicians (whom if
I were to call the Orpheuses of our age, I would not deviate from the truth in the slightest)
held within private walls; these men, in order to give a specimen
of the faculty they professed, somewhat more excellent than usual,
wished me alone to be a conscious witness of their arcane and scarcely
heard method and skill of playing. Therefore, with everything elegantly
prepared for exhibiting the specimen, and the place and time opportunely
appointed, they began a symphony, which

[Marginal note: Music producing wondrous effects.]
was performed on two smaller lutes, and a lute, which they call a Theorbo,
with such a harmony of concord, with such unusual distinctions of uncommon
intervals, that although I can confess to having explored something quite
excellent in Music; yet I do not remember having perceived anything similar,
for while they mix diatonic with chromatic, and these with enharmonic
modulations; it can scarcely be said how much the unusual mixture of these
genres stirred the affections of the soul. For now, as by a descending
diapason from a high note to a low one, gradually fading,

gradually fading away with a descending diapason from a high note to a low one, they thus affected the listener's soul with a certain languor; and by an ascent, as if awakening from a deep sleep, they stimulated it to undertake I know not what arduous task, now with a thin and subtle drawing of the bow, while they scraped the strings, they seemed to stir the spirit of the throbbing heart along with them, sometimes with a somewhat sad murmur of indignation they stirred the emotion to I know not what mournful and lamentable thing, you would say you were present at a tragic scene; soon from the somewhat sad modulation, gradually from relaxed to dense, intense, and full of joy and triumph chromatics, they swept me away with such impetus that I was almost overwhelmed by a certain frenzied madness; then rising into I know not what tumultuous and full of vehement ferocity, with alternating pursuits they incited the soul to battles and fights, and finally, with the impetus relaxed, they moved it to I know not what peculiar sweet affection, to compassion, divine love, and contempt for the world, with such grace and majesty of charm, that I am plainly persuaded that those ancient Heroes Orpheus, Terpander, and other musicians most famous by name among posterity, never attained a similar artistry. Therefore, the soul, imbued with this truly incomparable symphony, was carried away by a certain exotic emotion into the wondrous harmony of the celestial spheres; here I contemplated the laws of agreement and disagreement of all and individual bodies of this world, so ordered that while individual things abound in consonant-dissonances, yet all things in all things tend towards con-

various colored precious stones as there were orbits of wandering stars were
seen inserted: a wondrous work to behold; his left hand carried a measuring
rod, exquisitely crafted with gem-like artistry and distributed with wondrous skill.

They are encompassed, from all sides they trouble me, and as if by certain reflected rays of your divinity, they stimulate me day and night, that I may know you, love you, God my creator. But what do we love, when we love you by knowing you? Is it some bodily form? Or the revolutions of time? Or the brightness of the light of celestial bodies? Or the sweet melodies of harmonies? Is it the sweet scent of flowers and aromas? Or the delights of nectar and ambrosia? Or embraces pleasant and soft to the touch? Far be it, we do not love things like these, while we love you, our God; but we love a certain light brighter than all the bodies of the World, a certain voice sweeter than all harmonic sweetness, and a certain scent not to be compared with all the scents of the World, and food more pleasing than all the delicacies of human delights; finally, a certain embrace of the inner man, more delightful than all the pleasures of the World. Where shines for my soul that which no place contains, and where sounds that which time does not snatch away, and where smells that which no breath scatters, and where tastes that which gluttony does not diminish, and where clings that which satiety does not tear away. This truly is, to seek, to know, to love our God. But what then is this, O most benevolent lover of men? I asked the earth and the order of all living things; I heard the abysses and the countless creeping things of the living, and they answered, "We are not your God, seek above us;" I asked the sweet whispers of the stable air, and they said, "no." is a character in the book *The Man in the Moone* by Francis Godwin. He is the narrator and protagonist of the story. The name "Theodidactus" means "taught by God" in Greek, which is fitting for a character who embarks on a journey of discovery and encounters new knowledge.

In the story, Theodidactus is a Spanish gentleman who, after a series of unfortunate events, finds himself stranded on an island. He then invents a flying machine and travels to the Moon, where he encounters a utopian society of lunar inhabitants. The book is considered one of the earliest works of science fiction and explores themes of scientific discovery, religious tolerance, and social commentary.

The character of Theodidactus serves as a vehicle for Godwin to present his ideas about astronomy, cosmology, and the possibility of extraterrestrial life. Through Theodidactus's experiences, Godwin challenges conventional beliefs and encourages readers to consider new perspectives on the universe.

Theodidactus is portrayed as an intelligent, curious, and adventurous individual who is open to new experiences and willing to question established norms. His journey to the Moon represents a metaphorical journey of intellectual exploration and the pursuit of knowledge beyond the confines of earthly understanding.

In summary, Theodidactus is the central character of *The Man in the Moone*, a pioneering work of science fiction, and his name reflects his role as a seeker of divine knowledge and a discoverer of new worlds.

It surrounds the circumference of the lunar globe, and together with the Moon's rotation, it is agitated in a circle with perpetual course and flow. These agitations occur most intensely when the globe has been struck by the normal influx of solar rays, which happens at the time of the full moon or new moon. [Marginal note: Wonders of the Lunar Ocean.] For since, as you heard above, the lunar water is wonderfully mobile, it happens that as soon as the Sun strikes it with a normal diffusion of rays, it is quickly reduced to extreme rarity, causing those vehement agitations both at the time of the full Moon on the facing side, and at the time of the new Moon on the averted side. Hence, while the agitated water of the Lunar Ocean is more vehemently dashed both against the opposing rocks and against the vast walls of mountains, of which, as you see, there are countless numbers; it is necessary that a dreadful agitation is thereby caused by the contrary motions. Added to the extreme mobility of the unstable lunar element is the daily motion of the Sun, by which the impelled sea acquires so much greater strength, the more perpendicular its position to the Sun has been. From this also arises that formidable sound; for indeed the dashing of the waves, both against the opposing rocks and against themselves, causes a certain wonderful agitation of the lunar air, or what is the same, of the lunar effluvium, from which that strange and unusual sound is produced. For you know from the similarity of earthly things that troubled water can by no means coexist with still air.

[Marginal note: Power of the Moon & influence.]
As for the second point; know that an inherent power exists in the entire Lunar globe, so that as soon as it has sent forth the rays of its powers into a moist subject, it immediately rarefies, expands, dilates, and fertilizes it, now more, now less, according to the position of the Moon in its orbit. §. II.

De visis in auersa à Sole Lunæ facie.

THEODIDACTVS. But O Cosmiel, divine Master; what, I ask, is the meaning of that long day on the Moon, during which, for a journey of now nearly fourteen days, we have seen neither night nor any stars? Certainly, it clearly appears that we are established in another World; for I experience everything to be different and unlike what it is in the terrestrial World, Cosmiel; you ought to know that we have always continued our journey along the path of the lunar equator, and since the lunar sphere always has half of its body turned towards the Sun, and we have followed the Moon's motion in its orbit, it is not surprising that we have always been exposed to the Sun's presence, and the most intense and utterly unbearable heat, which you experienced, and about which [Marginal note: A fourteen-day day on the Moon.] you complained so much, clearly testifies to this; for where the Sun is always present, there, with the daytime heat dominating, there can be no night, and where there is no night, there the splendors of the stars cannot be seen, being obscured by the greater light with its excessive intensity; but so that your desire may be satisfied, I will now show you both night and the entire collection of stars, according to the position and arrangement which it presents to those established on this lunar globe. But the phenomenon of the Sun astonished me more than words can express; for at different times, I perceived its different face, especially in the hemisphere of the Moon turned away from us, for now I observed it crescent, then half, finally full; the reason for this was none other than the bulge of the lunar body, which cut the face of the Sun in different ways according to the Moon's varying distance from the Sun. All these phases of waxing and waning light I also noticed in the globes of Venus and Mercury; I saw the diameter of Venus, when situated in perigee, as well as Mercury, of unusual magnitude, so that I often doubted whether I was looking at two Suns in the sky; but more fully on these things in what follows.

These things having been done, I thus addressed Cosmiel. O most faithful Leader, O most wise instructor; I have now seen the incomprehensible works of the Lord, which are numberless; enlighten, I pray, my weak intellect, so that what I do not grasp, I may learn from you, my all-knowing Master.

Have you ever seen a wheel by which knives are usually sharpened? If you pour water upon it when it is agitated with violent motion, it does not follow the wheel, but, lifted upwards by the violence of the impetus, it is dispersed into the air; you ought to believe the same would happen with the globe of the Sun, if it were composed of pure liquid; for while the solar body revolves from east to west around the globe of the earth within the space of a natural day, unless it were restrained by more solid particles as if by certain barriers, it could by no means subsist, but it would necessarily happen that by the excessive violence of the motion by which the said liquid globe is agitated in a circle by daily rotation, it would either be dispersed or, its power being scattered and confused, it would create a very tumultuous and strange appearance of the globe; indeed, the fervor of the undulating material, endowed with the highest mobility, would, from its excessive rapidity, reduce the Sun now into an oval, now into a rhomboid, now into some other figure perceptible to the eye, which, however, you know to be contrary to experience; Therefore, lest this so inconvenient thing impede the operations of the inflowing power in the nature of things, the provident moderator of all things, the nature of things, enclosed this fiery liquid within the channels of more solid parts, so that it, restrained as if in some truly admirable vessel, would by no means exceed the limits of its fervor. Hence you see that both the Northern and Southern parts for the most part, as well as the depth of the Solar body, are composed of more solid parts, like a certain skeletal structure proportioned to the whole globe, and which within itself, as if in a certain womb, contains the matter of brilliant liquid!

# Ecstatic Journey

**Theodidactus:** I have understood everything perfectly; indeed, through this visual experience, I seem to almost touch the truth of the matter with my own fingers. Furthermore, nothing remains except for you to explain to me how these globes illuminate Saturn.

**Cosmiel:** First, it must be noted that the globe of Saturn equals, if it does not exceed, the globe of Jupiter in size. It is immense in itself and 165 times larger than the Earth; for its diameter equals at least 11,262 hourly leagues <note>A "league" was a common unit of distance; an "hourly league" refers to the distance a person could walk in one hour, roughly 3 miles.</note> extended in length. Since it is so vast, the surface of such an exorbitant mass—being so far removed from the Sun—could not be sufficiently illuminated by it.

<margin>
How these two companions illuminate Saturn.
</margin>

For this reason, Nature has provided it with two other "substitute suns"—that is, bodies of a solar nature—lest the huge mass of this worldly globe, destitute of sufficient light and heat, should seem to have been established in the nature of things in vain. These are the two globes which, like two substitute suns, are both versatile around their own centers and circle Saturn at an always equal distance from one another, so that no part of the huge globe remains deprived of the benefit of their light. 

However, notwithstanding the illumination of these companions circling always under one and the same parallel, such a huge mass would still suffer in its polar regions, condemned to perpetual darkness. Therefore, by a sagacious arrangement of Nature, besides the fact that the globe of Saturn rotates around its own axis, it also tilts to some extent toward opposite parts of the world, so that nothing in this globe is so hidden that the light of these two globes does not reach it. And lest, by the slowness of these companions, the parts...

He describes the complex rotation and axial tilt of the planet designed to ensure even the polar regions receive light.</summary>

the globes <note>The "companion globes" or moons of Saturn</note> would suffer harm from being struck by the most oblique light of their companions; however, provision was made for this through a rotation around their own axis, completed in roughly a monthly space of time. By this rotation, other parts in need of light are placed beneath the luminous globes with a wonderful anticipation, while those parts already saturated with light are moved into the place of those needing light by a marvelous succession.

*Theodidactus:* But explain now, why the companion globes do not always strike Saturn with full light, but instead, as they are agitated around their own center, they turn now this, now that warmer and more luminous portion toward the planet.

*Cosmiel:* Truly, it is by the highest design; for by this alternation it happens that whatever has been more vehemently excited in certain places by a continuous pouring-on of light, is reduced to a necessary temperate state by the lessening of that light. And thus, what for the inhabitants of Earth is the alternation of days and nights, is in this globe the intensification and remission of light poured out from the two Saturnian attendants.

*Theodidactus:* But I ask you, my Cosmiel, does the illumination of the Sun not contribute something of its own light to this globe?

*Cosmiel:* On the contrary, it does; for since this globe consists of a certain slow-flowing liquid, not unlike quicksilver <note>original: "hydrargyro"; an early term for mercury</note>, it happens that the Sun—even if it is only seen under an angle of three minutes—nevertheless illuminates it significantly in the absence of the companions by pouring its light over the aforementioned material, which is otherwise most capable of receiving light. If this did not happen, Saturn would certainly vanish from the eyes of Earth-dwellers from time to time, having suffered a sort of eclipse from the absence of light; yet this is contrary to experience. -># Journey into the Firmament<-

<margin>The Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn, seen from the position of the firmament, appear motionless and always at the same distance.</margin>

**Didacus:** But what is this marvel? For I see neither the Sun, nor Jupiter, nor Saturn moving; they remain separated by almost the same distance from one another. **Cosmiel:** You should know that the distance of these globes from your eye is so great that the entire circumference of the solar heaven is compressed into a space nearly equal to the solar body itself—and the same applies to the heavens of the other mentioned globes. Hence, it is no wonder that they seem almost motionless, or even vanish entirely if they are smaller than the Sun and the other superior planets.

<margin>All stars of the firmament revolve in their own peculiar circles, just like the planets, yet they appear fixed due to excessive distance.</margin>

I would have you be persuaded that the same thing happens while you are standing on Earth considering the globes of the firmament; for they all seem to be separated by an equal distance and immutable intervals from one another. This, however, is false. All these bodies of the firmament—or stars—that you see perform their courses in vast circles, no differently than the Sun, the Moon, and the other lower planets. The reason their motion is not observed by those living on Earth is that inconceivable distance of said globes from the Earth, which swallows up all the circles of those globes as if they were gathered into a single point.

<margin>A comparison.</margin>

I propose this example to you: if you were to tie lit torches to several carriage wheels set some distance apart, experience teaches that although the torches change position for those watching nearby due to the revolution of the wheels, someone situated one or two leagues <note>A league is an old unit of distance, usually about 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers.</note> away would see neither the place, nor the position, nor the distance change. This is because the entire wheel, due to the excessive distance, is reduced to the size of the torch...

<summary>The protagonist Didacus questions why the planets appear stationary from the heights of the firmament, leading Cosmiel to explain the optical effects of vast astronomical distances. Cosmiel uses the analogy of torches on distant carriage wheels to illustrate why moving celestial bodies appear fixed to a distant observer.</summary>

**Journey into the Firmament. 287**

...[He is] without limits, so He willed the world to be immense, as much as the material condition of things in this state permitted them, indeed as much as it could and should be; not that He could not have made it greater, but because the power of a corporeal creature, which has limitation from itself and its own nature, could not sustain a greater extension; just as your Philosophers and Theologians, while they ask whether God can actually create an infinite (thing), many rightly and wisely respond, that no; not that they think the infinite power of the Creator is exhausted, but because that implies a contradiction on the part of matter. *Theodid:* Stop, stop, my Cosmiel, I desire to see nothing more, for I fear lest I be overwhelmed by the excessive majesty of the Creator's glory; for I prefer to serve Him with humble obedience of mind, and with fear and trembling, than to scrutinize more curiously His incomprehensible works, of which there is no number, nor end. Take, take my soul, (Theodidactus's ecstatic apostrophe.) for now nothing more of sensible things delights me, I desire to be joined to Him with eternal love, who has wrought such great things in the nature of things for me, a most vile worm of the earth, I desire to be concentrated on Him with the whole affection of my mind, to adhere solely to Him, never to be torn away from Him. O my God, life of my soul, if You have built so great a structure for the sake of man alone, how great will be the immensity of invisible goods which You have prepared for Your beloved ones? For now indeed, in the ecstasy of my mind, I can exclaim, "*Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him.*"

--- Page 570 ---
288           Of the Ecstatic Journey

For the nations *themselves*. O Earth-born, sons of men, again
I say, why do you love vanity, and seek false-
hood; behold, behold these inestimable
mansions of the heavens; consider with your whole heart how
much God has created for the glory of man alone, even if un-
seen and hidden from us, yet for His own ends known to Him alone!
Live always with that disposition of mind in the enjoyment of this
fleeting light; so that, when the burden of the
flesh is finally laid aside, in that great and super-mundane Arche-
type, never exhausted, you may contemplate Him,
who is the center of our soul, the center of the entire
universe, the end and ultimate blessedness; who therefore may be
blessed forever, loved without end,
praised without limit for ages of ages.
Amen.

DIALOGUE II.
*Concerning the Providence of God shining forth*
*in the creation of the World.*
Speakers: Cosmiel &

CHAPTER I.

*Concerning the creation of the World.*

COSMEL. Come now, Theodidactus, it is now time that, having surveyed the globes of the World, and traversed the immense boundaries of the ocean of the Universe, you be restored to your globe by your return, so that you may make your Earth-dwellers participants in the secrets of nature, which you have learned from me. *Theodid.* Ah
                                  O o                                  mi

my divine Master, how much you dismay my soul with this
your voice! For indeed, to be separated from you, to me
is a thing even harder than death itself; let my soul rather die
the death of the just, so that, freed from the defilement of this
[Marginal note: Theodidactus's contention with Coſmiel.]
earthly contagion, it may always live with you, with you that

I promise that I will always be present to you in all your actions.
Theodid. Just as I have always conformed myself to your
will, which is God's, so now, if ever, I will subscribe to your
command, desiring nothing ever, except what you shall
judge to be for my salvation, and the greater good of my soul.
This one thing I will most earnestly contend from you, that
before you restore me to my globe, you prepare a solution
for certain doubts, which for a long time have tormented my
mind concerning the fabric of the world, and the reasons of divine
providence, by which it governs the Universe. Coſmiel. As you, my
son, have asked a most just thing, so I would be unjust if I did not
comply with your wishes. Be of good courage, confidently
ask me whatever your soul desires, and I would wish you to
consider yourself not so much prompt to ask, as me prompt to answer.
Theod. I accept your so benign [attitude] towards your

de mundi creatione . 291

your will; but lest I wander confusedly in a business otherwise most intricate, I will first propose to you some things concerning the making of the world, then concerning the supreme providence of God, by which He incessantly governs the world and all its parts, however hidden; thirdly and finally, concerning the wonderful providence by which He directs the human race to its ultimate end. Moreover, it will be your task to pervade my darkened mind with the light of your teaching, so that I may understand what you wisely answer to each point. Coſmiel.

Do not doubt, son, it will be as you requested.

Theodid. What then properly was that mass of darkness, which the sacred text calls "earth without form and void," which God, the Best and Greatest, created in the beginning of things? I wish to know. Coſmiel. Know that the matter proposed is of greater consideration than can be described in a few words, wherefore I begin from a deeper point. God, whose power has no end nor number, in the ineffable counsel of His decree, had conceived the world from eternity, and the world in God Himself was nothing other than God; therefore the full measure of time came, when it pleased Him to unfold the conceived world outwardly. First, by the immense and inscrutable power of His virtue, in the high point of eternity, by the sole efficacy of His infinite will, He created heaven and earth out of nothing: and although I am not unaware that some commentators of the sacred text understand by "heaven" in this place, the Empyrean Heaven; God's vast and immense palace, the seat of angels and blessed humans

[Marginal note: Gen. 1.]

to understand a dwelling place, which I do not deny, but nevertheless something more is indicated by it; that is, that immense interval, the space and place of the entire mundane fabric, in which, according to the eternal disposition of His providence, He had decreed to order the mundane globes—a space, I say, long, wide, deep—He produced:
[Marginal note: What is understood by the name of heaven.] no differently than a certain King about to lead forth a great army, first considers a place capable of such a multitude, in which he may arrange camps, direct battle lines, aptly distribute the individual ranks of the legions into their members, and train them to perform their duties properly. Therefore, space for such an army of globes, for aptly distributing the camps of the celestial militia, was especially necessary, and this is called heaven.
[Marginal note: What by the empty and void Earth,] *But the earth was without form and void, and darkness was*
*upon the face of the deep;* by this empty and void earth and abyss of darkness, nothing else is understood than that chaotic mass, or that immense chaos, pregnant with a mixture of all those seminal principles by which the world was afterwards to be formed: and just as nothing as yet ordered, nothing distinct, nothing constituted in its own proper form was found in it, so all things lay confused into one, all unformed, without any order or distinction, without any discrimination of forms, as if enveloped in a certain dark abyss. In which state of affairs, so that at last individual things, aptly distributed in their own places, might be furnished with their proper forms,
[Marginal note: What the primordial light of the world is.] behold, the voice of God resounded; *Let there be light*, and light was the primordial form of the world, which, as the greatest of all,

--- Page 575 ---
de creatione mundi . 293

most necessary for the world, inasmuch as without which
the world, condemned to eternal darkness, could not
have subsisted, so it ought to precede the appearance
of all other forms. This light, moreover, was
like a certain preceding material for the globes of light to be
formed in the world, and it was nothing else than a certain
radical heat, afterwards implanted in all bodies of the world,
by which alone they are formed and sustained;
it was luminous, so that it might bring into view
the whole apparatus of subsequent forms. You now have the first
active principle of all nature, that luminous
heat, the unique origin and root of the generation of things;
but since that heat was not sufficient,
unless another principle were prepared, with
which, mixed, it might perfect the generations of all things; [marginal note: What is water.]
hence the sacred text immediately at the beginning mentions the waters,
over which the Spirit of God was brooding; and
it was the radical moisture, the passive principle of things,
from which two principles, heat and moisture, all
kinds of beings that are in the world have their
origin. These things having been presupposed, the wisest
Creator soon girded himself for the distinction of parts
and the establishment of the rudiments of the mundane globes; [marginal note: Distinction of the parts of the world.]
which indeed were accomplished in this manner: the Divine
voice resounding, "Let there be a firmament in the midst
of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters";
soon all that terrestrial matter which before lay confused
and squalid in that chaotic mass, aroused by the voice
of the Lord, was distinguished into innumerable portions
of the world, and thus fur-

each portion obtained a place in the mundane fabric proportionate to the actions and duties for which they were destined; but since, immersed and weighed down by immense moisture, they could confer no benefit to the world; hence by the command of divine wisdom, [Marginal note: Distribution of water.] the waters were gathered into one place, and the dry land appeared, that is, for each mundane globe now firmed and solidified with terrestrial substance, a portion of water receded from that great chaos of moisture, which, partly distributed among the channels of the globes, partly relegated to the outermost confines of the world, left the firmament, that is, the celestial space of the globes established by eternal law, empty of waters, and thus, two other principles of things, cold and dry, emerged. *Theodidactus.* Wait a moment, Cosmiel; for a great doubt presses upon me, from which I deeply desire you to free me; what you say seems to openly disagree with sacred scripture; *For God said: Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear;* I certainly understand nothing else by "dry land" in this place [Marginal note: Objection.] than our earth; how then do you say that water was distributed not only to the earth, but also to each of the other mundane globes; for the sacred text does not say: let the waters be gathered into diverse places, but into one place? *Cosmiel.* You have indeed raised a significant doubt, which has not a little perplexed the minds of many; therefore, I will teach you how it is to be understood. Know therefore, that the principal end of God, Thrice Best, Greatest, in constituting the world was; firstly, glory

He was about to create; for in vain would the corporeal world

for whose sake all other things were created, was first
to be named, while the other globes, destined to serve it,
were named only implicitly. The terrestrial globe, as a kind of prototype
of the others; whence, on account of the purpose for which it was destined,
it was deservedly the most excellent of all mundane globes,
and endowed with a greater abundance and variety of all things necessary
for human life; [Marginal note: Of the excellent terrestrial globe.]
for the other globes, as servants, were endowed primarily with those gifts of nature

indeed, the terrestrial globe far surpasses them by an infinite
variety of forces, properties, and entities, not only
devoid of soul, but also of vegetative and sentient
nature, in variety and abundance.

This is not the condition of this fleeting time, but it is reserved for that state in which you will contemplate Him face to face in the Word of life:

And although the world is such and so great, nevertheless, He ordered it with such order and proportion, regarding each mundane globe, that no body so small is found in it, which does not correspond to another, and all things to each other, with perfect union and most absolute harmony. On the distance of the globes. 325

the rays of the Sun, reflected differently and differently onto the earth, clearly teach us, producing different effects under the frigid zone, another under the temperate, and finally another constitution under the torrid zone, as you have extensively demonstrated in the Art of Anacamptics; and if this admirable variety of diverse effects is so harmonious that the Earth, unable to be preserved without it, would introduce perpetual dissonance into things; therefore, the distance of the Earth from the Sun, with such and such a magnitude of body, produces such a disposition of the Earth and no other, such a temperament and no other, such a harmonious variety and no other.
Again, this distance, with such a magnitude of the Earth, produces a most equal portion of light and shadow in all places, as you have shown in many ways in the aforementioned art of Anacamptics. But if the distance were greater or smaller, then the whole harmony would be reduced to a certain most confused dissonance; just as strings, consonant under such and such a length, as soon as they deviate from their proper length, produce I know not what inharmonious and dissonant sound instead of melody. Thus, if the Earth, with the same magnitude, were nearer to the Sun, or further from it, than it actually is; being nearer, struck by more efficacious rays of the Sun, or being further, struck by weaker rays, besides introducing the greatest inequality of light and shadow, would also produce a temperament for human life not only harmful, but also utterly incongruous.       However, because the most fervent Sun together with the most humid Moon could not establish a perfect harmony of humors in the terrestrial globe without the intervention of other bodies, hence divine providence established between the Moon and the Sun two other mundane bodies, namely Venus and Mercury, bodies excelling in diverse virtues, in which the vehemence of the solar rays might be as if tempered and blunted [marginal note: What Venus and Mercury achieve], and thereby, with increased powers necessary for lunar humidity, it might bless the Earth with greater variety. For the influence of the Venusian body, excelling in a certain fecundative power, communicated to the Moon, similarly fertilizes its humidity. But Mercury, a separator of the consonant from the dissonant, tempers what is harmful and superfluous, drawn into itself from both the Sun and Venus, and thus finally establishes another kind of harmony necessary for the lower world; all of which, in the course of time, according to the various aspects and eccentric positions of the said planets, always bring about diverse combinations of effects; because furthermore no instrument is so perfectly constructed that it does not, in the course of time, with strings either loosened or tightened more than is right, incur dissonance [marginal note: How the diseases of the globes are cured]. **Concerning the distance of the globes, 331**

& having completed a full circulation of tones, they would return. But since the parts of the globes or planetary bodies are heterogeneous, and have obtained diverse natures, qualities, properties, and powers on account of their diverse position and relation to the other surrounding Planets, Nature willed them to revolve around their own center, so that they would always turn different parts towards the Earth, and would accomplish the same thing in celestial Music that the combination of dissonances with consonances achieves in artificial Music.

You see therefore that the Planets are arranged in such an order that if even one recedes from its determined limit, as it were a harmonic interval, the whole harmony is deservedly destroyed. *Theod:* I have understood everything very well that you have discussed concerning divine providence regarding the arrangement of the planets; But I do not understand how this arrangement concerning bodies lying hidden in that inexplicable depth of the firmament is to be understood, since I find no proportion of such bodies to the earth, inasmuch as they are established beyond all range of the human eye. *Cosmiel:* Theodidactus, you have asked a difficult thing of me, which indeed it would scarcely be permissible for me to explain to you, except through certain very profound principles not obvious to everyone, which nevertheless are most true, and soon you will clearly see that although the world is inconceivable and immeasurable, and the mundane globes are innumerable, nevertheless all things in all [Marginal note: All things are in all things.] things, individual things in individual things, whatsoever in whatsoever exist by an ineffable reason, and all things are connected to each other by an admirable bond and proportion, with a reciprocal exchange of influences

Know that the Universe is the very structure of all created things, and that anything receives all things in such a way that in it they are itself in a contracted manner; for since anything cannot actually be all things, but rather exists in a contracted state, it contracts all things so that they are itself; if therefore all things are in all things, all things seem to precede anything. Therefore all things are not multiple, because that plurality does not precede anything; whence all things without plurality preceded anything by the order of nature; therefore there are not multiple things in anything existing, but all things without plurality are that very same thing. However, the Universe exists only in a contracted manner in things, and every actually existing thing contracts the universals so that they are actually that which it is; but everything actually existing is in God, because He is the act of all things, and act is the perfection and end of potency; whence, since the Universe is contracted in every actually existing thing, it is clear that God, who is in the Universe, is in anything and everything.

CHAPTER VIII.
On the Empyrean Heaven.

THEODIDACTUS. Just as nothing is more commonplace in the Schools concerning the Empyrean Heaven, so I find nothing more obscure and unknown than it. Therefore, I ask you, my Cosmiel, you who have hitherto displayed the structure of the entire world to my eyes, do not hesitate to show me that greatest and most excellent dwelling place of all the world. Cosmiel. Ah, my Theodidactus, you truly do not know what you ask. Do you think a man clothed in mortal flesh can approach the supreme court of the world, the seat of God, Angels, and the elect, or that it can be surveyed by eyes defiled by worldly impurities? That is not reserved for the state of this fleeting life, but for eternal happiness. Theodid: Forgive my rashness, and my exceedingly, indeed, overly bold, not to say presumptuous, curiosity. Thus, with divine grace inspiring me, I propose to live in the future, so that, when the debt of mortal flesh is paid, I may deserve to behold it in a much more eminent way than with fleshy eyes. Nevertheless, you will not omit to answer some doubts that occur to me concerning this heaven, so that in some way, my desire for knowledge may be satisfied.

Hence God is so far from having created infinite worlds, that rather, besides this one, He should be considered to have created no other. If the latter, then something would be lacking to those worlds; nor would they contain the entire fullness of corporeal perfection, which can by no means be said. CHAPTER X.
Concerning the Consummation and Restoration of this sensible world.

COSMIEL. I said above that the sensible world is balanced between two (ages), of which the former age lacks a beginning and ends in the first instant of the creation of all things; the latter age has a beginning but lacks an end, whose beginning is to be taken from the principle of the renewal of all things, that is, after the last judgment of the eternal Judge has been pronounced. Therefore, the space of time between both ages consists only of a beginning and an end, inasmuch as the world, unstable in its successive flux, is considered subject to corruptions and genera-
[Marginal note:] Two ages, together with time, constitute all eternity.
tions. A double age is joined by time, just as two lines extended infinitely on both sides by a certain point; for just as there is no proportion of a point to a line, so there is no proportion of time, however long, to eternity, which the two lines joined by the point of time denote. *Why God, although He created so much for the sake of man, yet so few attain eternal salvation, and concerning the hidden judgments of God.*

# CONCLUSION
# OF THE WORK
### With the Author's protestation.

[Decorative initial H in a square frame with floral motifs] AVE, kind Reader, in this
Ecstatic Journey you have my opinion concerning the fabric and
composition of the World and celestial bodies, indicated under the covering and veil of a feigned rapture.
I would ask this one thing of you: that you do not perhaps interpret the rather bold introduction to this work in a negative light; but rather, I would wish you to persuade yourself that it was done for no other purpose than to instill the doctrine of an unusual subject into the reader's mind with a more pleasant and sweeter reasoning. My aim was that the mind, being rendered more attentive to each thing proposed and answered back and forth, would thus become more eager for what was to follow. Indeed, I did not hope to achieve this better than by following the genius of poets and tragedians. I aimed to present these narrations concerning the vast dwellings of the world, transacted through the introduced persons of Cosmiel and Theodidactus, and explored through simulated raptures into the innermost parts of higher nature, and in this way, as it is said, provoke enthusiasm with enthusiasm; if besides, perhaps some descriptions [decorative flourish] un-

--- Page 727 ---
**Conclusion.** 445

If the Reader finds them expressed **more symbolically**; I would like him to attribute it to the ardor of a restless intellect playing in the manner of poets, for thus the purpose of the matter proposed to us demanded.
   *While my wandering mind may not be my own*
Indeed, I considered no kind of writing more effective for captivating the Reader's mind and for fixing it to ponder the proposed matters with deeper reasoning. But as for the opinions concerning physical truths, let no one think me to be of such brazen audacity, of such stubborn mind, that I should attempt to impose the tenets asserted in this Work, established by the irrefutable weight of arguments, **more manifestly** as a rule of evangelical truth, as it is usually said. Far be such confidence from a religious heart; for neither have I ever allowed a similar stain of **self-love** to settle in my mind. I know that saying of the Wise Man: *All things are difficult, and they cannot be explained by speech*; I know that however much anyone may have progressed in investigating the paths of divine Wisdom, he will always find himself so much further from the goal of truth, the closer he has approached; and so many more things remain for him to learn, the more he knows. Wherefore, as there are a thousand opinions of men, a thousand differences of minds, so to each one I leave the freest will and judgment in this Work to think what he wishes: This one thing I say, whoever knows the secrets of the analogical art, he will most truly discover that this one (art) has been **granted** to the weakness of human intellect as a kind of key by the bounty of divine gift.

--- Page 728 ---
446          An Ecstatic Journey

to be granted, by which access is granted to us to the inner sanctuaries of a celestial and more sublime nature, and he will openly confess the truth of that old saying, *All things exist in all things (in their own way)*. Having used this in this Work, I seem, unless I am mistaken, to have uncovered some knowledge of celestial philosophy, so abstruse, by which, if the Reader likewise uses it, even if he has not entirely reached the goal of truth, I believe he will at least not stray far from it. Be that as it may, just as I have composed this Ecstatic Journey and the hidden truths within it solely for the honor and glory of eternal Wisdom and the benefit of souls, so also I wish everything in it to be subjected to the judgment of the Holy Roman Church, which is the sole infallible rule of truth, with the humblest obedience of mind.

I have not brought forward new or paradoxical things, but I have derived them, driven by the efficacy of consequent reasons, as certain corollaries from those things which other most noble writers before me have already stated, whom I have partly cited in the exhortatory epistle, and partly will cite below; but so that I may explain myself with a certain concatenated sorites of inferences, I have argued thus: If that immense expanse of the heavens, with all solidity of spheres banished, is filled with a fluid and ethereal aura, as is now almost the common and most true opinion, and confirmed by the calculations of almost all Astronomers from many years of observations; therefore the bodies of the stars moved in it, (since they cannot subsist otherwise,) no otherwise

--- Page 729 ---
Concluſio. 447

...no differently than the earth, they subsist by their own centers; therefore, the parts of each globe or Star will partly flow together to its own proper center by natural appetite, and partly flow out from it. If this is true, then just as there is an attraction of solid parts to their center, so also there is an expulsion of light parts exhaled from the same. Therefore each consists of its own atmospheres; if (they have) atmospheres, therefore moisture cannot be absent from them; if (they have) moisture, therefore also solid matter, which contains the moisture as if in some vessel. But these cannot be preserved without heat dissolving the moisture, nor this (heat) without the concurrence of mediating air. Therefore all and each must be composed of the four elements, each endowed with a peculiar prerogative in accordance with the nature of its acquired position. If this is true, then from these, no differently than from all mixed things, an emanation of diverse properties, forms, and influences will result, with a perpetual vicissitude of alterations, which continuous generation and corruption must necessarily follow. Therefore, the Stars are subject to corruptions, because they are subject to alterations; they are subject to alterations, because they are mixed; they are mixed, because they are elementary, because they possess solid, humid, aerial, and fiery or hot (elements). If they are elementary, therefore they have an atmosphere agitated by the confluence of heavy and light (parts); therefore they consist of their own centers; therefore, that they are bound to solid spheres cannot happen; therefore they move in a liquid; therefore the heaven is liquid and permeable everywhere, which was to be demonstrated. You see therefore, with the heaven assumed to be liquid, all that has been said from the con-

It is asked first, however, what in fact this roughness and flatness of the Moon really is, that is, from what material it consists, and to what material it can most rightly be compared. Response: the tuberous and unequal part of the Moon, brighter than others, can be more suitably accommodated to the earth itself and its continent than to any other known earthly things, for it receives almost all earthly qualities in itself. It is not, however, that anyone should therefore think that the Moon is composed of such sand, mud, or stone as this earth of ours, since perhaps it can consist of another material, entirely different from our imagination, and in a manner still incomprehensible. All this I boldly affirm, that these protuberant and rougher, and brighter parts can be better compared to nothing here on earth than to a continent, for which reason we shall henceforth call this land. But as for the lower places of the Moon, clearly, those great spots, which perpetually appear darker to us than the mountainous places, are no less congruously equated with our Oceans, seas, lakes, ponds, and marshes, which also have their windings, bays, and promontories; I by no means assert, however, that these Lunar waters are similar to ours, but that we have nothing here on earth more similar to them, due to the great affinity of both, with which we can compare them. Therefore, I conclude that the clearly illuminated surface is land, and the darker spots are waters, as Kepler also concedes in his dissertation: with Galileo's Sidereal Messenger.

Concerning the lunar body, it must be said that it is a terrestrial globe, consisting partly of fluid and watery parts, and partly of solid and dry parts; this is first suggested by its appearance, which it presents for observation through telescopic instruments. For the shadowy or spotted parts, and those less suffused with light, are best explained if they are said to be watery; the more illuminated parts are solid and consistent, which great unevenness and the prominences of mountains clearly declare. For they could not remain in such a stable state if they were fluid. Also concerning the center of the Moon and other celestial bodies. fol. 611. it should nonetheless be credited to them; it was a matter of

--- Page 743 ---
Conclusion. 461

And let these Authorities suffice for establishing our opinion. Innumerable others could have been added, but lest the little work should exceed the due limits of its size, I decided to acquiesce in these few among many. But whoever shall have desired the said things treated more extensively, I advise him to consult the works of the Authors contained in the following table; nor let the Reader be disturbed if he finds some things handed down in this little work to be more paradoxical; for I would wish him to persuade himself that, just as different paths of philosophizing have been established for me from the common, so I cannot approve the simplicity of some who hold and believe so sacrosanctly what they have been taught from childhood, or what Aristotle prescribed to them, that they think nothing is to be admitted other than what "he himself said," indeed, I have not infrequently wondered that some even among the Orthodox have more faith in a Pagan Philosopher (whose whole study seems to have been placed in this, whose entire weight and strength of arguments concerning celestial philosophy seems to have looked to this end, that he might assert his opinion about the eternity of the world, so contrary to Christian Doctrine) than they have in either Sacred Scripture or the decrees of the Holy Fathers, its interpreters. Therefore, having abandoned opinions unworthy of a Christian Philosopher, I, having examined the principles of the philosophy of the world by long and persistent study according to the rule of the combinatorial and analogical art, from the admirable connection of all things, and the necessary dependence of all things on individual things, and of individual things on all things, have deduced some consequences, as I said, which, although to some per-

--- Page 744 ---
462   Conclusion of the Ecstatic Journey.
strange to some, yet they are truly not dissimilar, and necessarily follow from infallible deduction (assuming the truth of the observations). He alone will discover this who, free from all disturbance, according to the balance of truth, has more accurately weighed both our testimonies and those of the illustrious men adduced in this Work.
